- `reassign {id, holder}` moves a held task. A task nobody holds is refused `not_held`. A move from agent to agent, agent to subtree and subtree to agent are all allowed.
- `status {id, status}` changes the state; it can also set `versions`, `source_version` and `fork_from`, and then `status` may be left out. `report {id, from?, state?, result?, usage?}` records the last report on the task. `list` and `get` read tasks; `get` also returns the ids of the task’s children.

Every change of holder, including the one given at `add`, appends `{from, to, by, at}` to `history`. `by` is the caller, or `null` for the operator. The history is the audit of who held the task and when.

one history step (illustrative values):

```
{"from": "lead-a", "to": {"subtree": "team-b"}, "by": "lead-a", "at": 1.7e9}
```

*Animation: Who holds the task* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/agents/agentic-resources/tasks.mp4). add creates t1 with source gh:o/r#12 and no holder. assign gives it to lead-a, and a second assign is refused with already_held. reassign moves it to the subtree of team-b. The history lists both steps as from, to, by and at.

#### Who writes, and where it is stored

The registry has one rule of its own: in `report`, `from` defaults to the caller and must be the caller or one of its descendants, else `not_in_subtree`. Everything else is the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/). Only a branch lead is granted the write verbs `add`, `assign`, `reassign`, `status` and `report` on the registry. A worker sends its lead the `agentic_resources` `report` message, and the lead writes the registry.

The registry keeps no tasks in memory. Its record names a store agent in `task_store_id`, and each write appends one snapshot row `{kind: "task", task_id, content: <entry>}` to it. Every read takes the latest row per `task_id`, so a restart rebuilds the tasks from the store. A store that refuses or cannot be reached gives `store_refused`, and nothing falls back to RAM.

The store may be volatile (`ram_store`) or a durable one. The wiring is explicit, as for agent memory: the registry’s `can_call` reaches the store, and the store’s `callable_by` lists the registry. The registry serializes the writes of one registry agent, so two leads cannot race. [State and durability](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/state/) covers what survives a restart.

Sources: agentic_resources: spawn, limits, report (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-agentic-resources/src/lib.rs#L348); agentic_resources: role cards (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-agentic-resources/src/cards.rs#L52); agentic_resources readme (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-agentic-resources/src/readme.md#L1); agentic_resources: the same verbs in Python (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/agentic_resources/src/agentic_resources/tools.py#L197); task_registry: assign, reassign, report (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-task-registry/src/lib.rs#L555); agentic_resources: tool grants opened on the tool’s end (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-agentic-resources/src/lib.rs#L766); task_registry: versions, source_version, fork_from, usage (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-task-registry/src/lib.rs#L24); task_registry readme (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-task-registry/src/readme.md#L1); task_registry: the same verbs in Python (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/task_registry/src/task_registry/tools.py#L1); where the host registers both (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-cli/src/main.rs#L116)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/

The canvas is an example of building on the kernel. `fantastic canvas` serves a page from the binary where you build, run and wire systems visually with an AI, and every part of it is an agent.

#### A page that is a kernel

The page is its own kernel in the browser, bridged to the host kernel through the `canvas_ws` leg. It holds no memory and no AI. Every cell is a **view** of a host agent, such as a terminal, an AI chat, a python agent or an MCP server, or page-side content (`html`, `gl`).

*Animation: Every cell is a view of an agent* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/cells.mp4). The canvas page is its own kernel in the browser, bridged to the host kernel through canvas_ws. Each cell on the page is a view of a host agent: a terminal shows an exec_bridge job, a chat shows an AI agent. The page holds no memory and no AI.

Double-clicking opens the selector, which lists everything that can be placed there. In the README’s words: “Nothing floats on the canvas; every surface is a cell.”

`new_canvas {name}`, sent to a canvas, makes a **child** canvas under it, and deleting a canvas deletes the canvases it spawned. Each canvas shows only its own subtree and the agents under no canvas. `user`, and every AI under a canvas, may call every host agent with every verb (granted on both sides); you narrow it with `update_agent`.

In this part: User (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/user/); Canvas (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/); Views of agents (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/); HTML and GL agents (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/html-gl/); Skin and backgrounds (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/skin/); Cabinet (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/cabinet/); Web MCP (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/web-mcp/); User home store (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/home-store/); Canvas page (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/page/); System agents (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/system/)

Sources: README.md: the canvas (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/README.md#L305); canvas.md (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/docs/canvas.md#L11); web.rs: the canvas tree, child canvases (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/web.rs#L1)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › User

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/user/

The kernel knows only agents, so the person at the keyboard is one too. It is called `user`, its handler is `user.tools`, and every call the terminal and the canvas make goes out through it. That makes `user` the sender: its grants are the ones checked, and replies route back to it.

This page covers what `user` does with a call from a canvas tab, why the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) judges it and not the tab, and the other verbs it answers: `around`, `path` and the inquiries. The canvas leg that carries the tab’s frames is in [Web agents](/fantastic/foundations/agents/web/#ws). The `user` agent described here is the one in the Rust canvas host.

#### One human, one agent

The agent id is `user`. In the terminal the code says the terminal “IS an agent on the spine, not a client of a server”, and its reads and acts go out as the **sender** `user`.

In the canvas tree `user` is the root of the host’s web agents: `web` is its child, and the canvas leg `canvas_ws` and the page server `canvas_page` sit under `web`. `user` also carries a `page_loader` field naming `web_loader`, the agent that holds the canvas page’s records.

the canvas host’s first agents:

```
user
└── web
    ├── canvas_ws
    └── canvas_page
```

A canvas tab never calls a host agent itself. The leg’s only call target is `user`: `user`’s `callable_by` names `canvas_ws` with `user`’s own verbs, and `canvas_ws`’s `can_call` is rewritten to `user`, plus each connected page’s own agents. Beyond that the leg holds only `watch` and `emit` on every agent, and `state_subscribe` on the root and the kernel. Every call to a host agent goes through `user`.

#### forward: the call leaves as user

The page wraps each call to a host agent as `forward {target, payload, timeout?}` (**forward** is the verb that carries a call) and sends it to `user`. A call addressed to `user` itself is sent as its own payload, unwrapped.

what the page sends user (illustrative target):

```
{"type": "forward", "target": "notes",
 "payload": {"type": "reflect"}}
```

`user` sends `payload` to `target` from inside its own handler, so the sender of that onward send is `user`. The reply comes back verbatim, binary bodies included. The verb needs a non-empty `target` string and a `payload` object, or it answers `bad_arg`; a `timeout` must be a number.

There is no default timeout. The call lasts as long as the target takes, which matters for an AI turn that runs for minutes. A `timeout` that is given is honoured, and a call that runs out with no result answers `timed_out`.

`forward` adds no secret marks of its own, so values travel and are recorded as they are. A secret mark the caller put under `payload` is carried onto the onward send, so [records](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/) mask it the same way. Who may call `forward` is `user`’s `callable_by` and nothing else.

*Animation: Every call goes out as user* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/user/forward.mp4). A canvas tab wraps its call as forward {target: "notes", payload: {type: "reflect"}} and sends it to user. user sends the payload to notes with its own id as the sender. notes replies, and the reply comes back to the tab verbatim, with no default timeout.

A tab checks at start that it is admitted. It sends `user.forward` of `reflect` to `kernel`, and if the answer’s reason is `unauthorized` the page shows the refusal and runs nothing else.

#### What the gate sees

Because the onward send is `user`’s, the call gate checks `user`’s `can_call` and the target’s `callable_by`, as it does for any send. The tab’s own rights do not enter into it.

The canvas host writes both edges for `user` by grants. `user`, the canvas’s AI agents and a few host helpers hold every agent on both edges, in the code’s words **god mode by grants**: the target’s `callable_by` names each holder and each holder’s `can_call` names the target. The human reshapes them with `update_agent`. A cabinet’s agents are not reached this way.

So narrowing `user`’s `can_call` is how the person limits what the canvas can do. The next `forward` is refused at egress, with the refusal the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) describes.

Every agent except stores and a cabinet’s agents may also `send` to `user`, on both edges, so that an exec agent’s monitor delivery, a sub-routine the AI built or an inquiry’s answer can reach it.

The reverse is refused. `send` is not a verb of the human, and `user` answers it with reason `unhandled` and the text “use `forward`”.

*Animation: The gate judges user’s grants* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/user/gate.mp4). With user.can_call and notes.callable_by both granting, a forward gets its reply. The person narrows user.can_call with update_agent and the next forward is refused at egress. A send to user itself is refused with reason unhandled: send is not a verb of the human.

#### around and path

`around {canvas?, view?, theme?, x, y, radius}` lists the cells of a page view that lie within `radius` of a point, nearest first. It reads the page records, defaulting to the main canvas, the view `view_root` and the theme `canvas`. A cell’s rectangle comes from the view’s layout for that theme.

around (shape; backend_id when the cell has one):

```
{"view": "view_root", "members": [{"id": …, "kind": …, "title": …,
  "rect": {"x": …, "y": …, "w": …, "h": …}, "distance": …, "backend_id": …}]}
```

Distance runs to the rectangle’s nearest edge and is 0 inside it. `x`, `y` and `radius` must be numbers with `radius` above 0, or the reply is `bad_arg`. An unknown view is `not_found`.

The caller’s own grants judge the result. A caller with no origin, the shell, sees every cell. Any other caller sees a cell only if its `can_call` holds an entry `<tree guid>|<id>` for the cell or an ancestor, or `<tree guid>|*`; `*|*` covers every tree.

`path {rescan?}` answers `{dirs, executables, self}`: the PATH directories, every executable on them by name with its full path, and the running fantastic’s own executable. PATH is this process’s merged with the login shell’s, because a CLI started from a service has a narrower one. The first directory wins, and `executables.fantastic` is always the running one.

The scan runs when `user` boots and stays in RAM; `rescan: true` scans again. What a name means, a coding agent or an editor, is for the caller to decide.

#### Inquiries: an agent asks the person

An agent that needs the person sends `user` an `inquiry {text, kind?, options?, request_id?}`. The `kind` is `text` (the default), `single`, `multi` or `confirm`; `single` and `multi` need `options`. Nothing suspends. `user` accepts it at once and holds it as open.

the inquiry reply (illustrative pid):

```
{"accepted": true, "re": 4655, "request_id": null, "open": 1}
```

`re` is the pid of the task the inquiry runs under, and it is the handle for the answer. `inquiries {asker?}` lists the open ones, oldest first, and the canvas shows each as a card in the asker’s chat.

`answer_inquiry {re, answer}` takes words, a list of picks or true or false. `user` sends the asker a `send` on its own thread, then closes the inquiry. If the answer does not reach the asker, the inquiry stays open and the reply is `refused`.

what the asker reads (illustrative pid):

```
[reply to 4655 · user inquiry]
<answer>yes</answer>
<request_id></request_id>
```

Open inquiries live in RAM only. A host restart forgets them, and the asker’s own history keeps the question.

*Animation: An inquiry is held, then answered* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/user/inquiry.mp4). The agent ai_1 sends user an inquiry of kind confirm. user answers {accepted: true, re: 4655} at once and holds it in RAM. The person calls answer_inquiry with re 4655 and yes, and ai_1 receives “[reply to 4655 · user inquiry]” with yes on its own thread.

#### The rest, and the Python twin

`user` also answers `export_subtree` and `import_subtree`, which write an agent and everything under it as a blueprint folder and bring one back as a live subtree. They are not covered here.

The Python `user.tools` answers only `reflect`, `export_subtree` and `import_subtree`. `forward`, `around`, `path` and the inquiries are verbs of the Rust canvas host.

Sources: user bundle: verbs, forward, around, the send refusal (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user/src/lib.rs#L1); inquiries: ask, list, answer (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user/src/inquiries.rs#L1); grants.rs: how page grants decide what around shows (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user/src/grants.rs#L1); path.rs: the human’s programs (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user/src/path.rs#L1); web.rs: the canvas tree and the leg that reaches only user (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/web.rs#L1); reach.rs: god mode by grants, and the way back (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/reach.rs#L1); user_bridge.ts: the page wraps every call as forward (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/user_bridge.ts#L1); Python user.tools (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/io/user/src/user/tools.py#L1)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › Canvas

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/

A canvas page holds one **view**, `view_root`, and the view owns the cells on it. The page kernel has no verbs that create or delete agents anywhere. The view answers them for its own cells, so a human and an AI change the canvas through the same messages.

This page covers those verbs, in the order you use them: `place`, `move`, `wire`, `hide`, `show` and `remove`, then the selector that a double-click opens. What a cell draws is covered in the other pages of this part.

#### The view owns its cells

The page’s root agent, `canvas`, has no editing verb; asked for one, it answers that the view is the one to talk to. It holds the one view, and the view’s cells are the view’s children. The view answers `place`, `move`, `fit`, `update`, `wire`, `remove`, `hide`, `show`, `open`, `tree`, `theme` and `terminal_renderer`.

The view is page-side TypeScript, packed into the binary. Calls reach it like calls to any agent, so the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) judges them. The address of the root view is `<page guid>|view_root` (see [the canvas overview](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/)).

#### Place: a new cell at x, y

A `place` names what to make and where. The `kind` is `html`, `gl`, `terminal` or `chat`, or a `handler_module` that names any page bundle. `x` and `y` are required numbers in view coordinates, and a call without them is refused with `reason: "bad_arg"`.

A `terminal` or `chat` cell needs a `backend_id`, the host agent it shows. A `place` with only a `backend_id` and no kind makes a view of that agent, drawn the way the agent’s own record says.

The cell gets the id you pass, or `<kind>_` and eight hex digits. An id that already exists is refused with `reason: "exists"`, and the hint says to `update` it or `remove` it first. A cell with no size starts at 480 by 320.

place an html cell (illustrative guid):

```
[{"target": "<page guid>|view_root", "payload": {"type": "place", "kind": "html", "x": 80, "y": 60, "bytes": "<b>hello</b>"}}]
```

The body of an `html` or `gl` cell is `bytes`, taken verbatim. An html body that is empty, a placeholder or truncated is refused with the reason. `place` and `update` set only `display_name`, `html`, `gl_source`, `trusted`, `readme`, `can_call` and `callable_by`, and a field `place` does not take comes back in `ignored`. If the html calls an agent that the cell’s `can_call` lacks, the reply names the missing grants.

*Animation: Place and move a cell* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/place.mp4). A send of place {kind: html, x: 80, y: 60} goes to view_root. The cell appears at 480 by 320, and its rectangle is written to layout_canvas. A move {id, x: 400} then rewrites only that rectangle. The cell itself is untouched.

#### Move: a position lives in the layout

A cell’s `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` are not on the cell. They are in the view’s **layout** for the theme in use: one `layout.ts` child agent per theme, named `layout_<theme>`, whose `rects` map a cell id to its rectangle.

a layout agent’s record (illustrative id):

```
layout_canvas   rects: {"html_1a2b3c4d": {"x": 80, "y": 60, "width": 480, "height": 320}}
```

`move {id, x?, y?, width?, height?}` rounds the values and merges them over the cell’s old rectangle in that layout. A `move` with no geometry is refused, and so is an id that is not a cell of this view. Dragging a cell by its head writes the same rectangle. `place` and `update` write their geometry there too.

There are two stock themes. `canvas` is the free two-dimensional canvas. `mobile` is one column, 400 wide, and `auto` (the default) picks `mobile` in a tab narrower than 768 px. `theme {name}` chooses one. Switching moves the cells, never the agents, because each theme has its own `rects`.

A cell with no rectangle in the theme in use is placed once by the layout. The free theme puts it in the nearest free space around the centre of what the tab shows, 24 px from other cells. The column puts it at the bottom.

#### Wire: write a grant on both cells

`wire {sender, receiver, verbs}` is a grant. It adds the verbs to the sender’s `can_call` for the receiver and to the receiver’s `callable_by` for the sender. It writes each side only when that side is a cell of this view, because another agent’s record is not the view’s to write. A host agent as receiver gets only the sender’s side.

The reply is `{wired: {sender, receiver, verbs}}`. The verbs are merged as a set, so a repeated `wire` adds nothing twice. A `wire` where neither agent is a cell of the view is refused with `not_found`. A `wire` without a sender, a receiver or a non-empty list of verbs is refused with `bad_arg`. The rule that decides whether the send then passes is the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/): both ends must grant it.

wire (illustrative ids):

```
[{"target": "<page guid>|view_root", "payload": {"type": "wire", "sender": "chart_1", "receiver": "feed_1", "verbs": ["watch"]}}]
```

*Animation: Wire, hide and show* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/wire.mp4). Cells chart_1 and feed_1 sit on the view. wire {sender: chart_1, receiver: feed_1, verbs: [watch]} adds watch to chart_1’s can_call and to feed_1’s callable_by. hide {id: feed_1} then takes feed_1 off the view and its agent keeps running, and show brings it back at the same place.

#### Hide, show and remove

Three verbs take a cell away, and they differ in what they leave. `hide {id}` takes the cell off the view. Its agent keeps running and its rectangles are kept. The id goes on the view’s own `hidden` list, which holds for every theme, so a reload keeps the cell hidden.

`show {id, x?, y?}` removes the id from that list and the cell mounts again, live. The `x` and `y` are used only when the cell was hidden. A cell that is already shown keeps its place, and `move` is the verb for moving it. `hide` and `show` refuse anything that is not a cell, such as the background, a selector or a layout.

`remove {id}` deletes the cell from the view and clears its hidden entry. The layout drops the rectangles of a cell that is gone. The click on a cell’s ✕ sends a hide. Shift+✕ and right-click then Delete delete the agent, and the head menu also offers Export…

#### The selector: a popup that is an agent

A double-click on empty canvas, or Ctrl-K (Cmd-K on a Mac), adds a **selector** agent at that spot. A double-click inside a cell’s frame does not. Its id is `selector_` and eight hex digits, and its record holds the spot in view coordinates (`x`, `y`) and on the screen (`sx`, `sy`).

The selector’s `boot` opens the popup on top of everything. When you pick a tile, press Esc or click away, the selector deletes itself, and what you picked is made at its spot. It is never a cell: the canvas draws no frame for it, and one left by a closed tab is removed when the page loads.

While it exists, anyone with the grant can send it `tiles {typed?}`. The reply is `{tiles: [{label, kind, section, hint}]}`, the kinds a cell can be made of here for that text. The tiles come in sections: `host`, `coding`, `bundles`, `page`, `page_bundles` and `chats`. The built-in ones are `terminal`, `python agent`, `mcp connector`, `user store`, `html`, `stream`, `file tree`, `preview`, `canvas theme` and `tips`, plus the AI agent tile. The `coding` section lists `fantastic`, `claude`, `codex`, `aider` and `opencode` when they are on your `PATH`.

*Animation: The selector popup* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/selector.mp4). A double-click on empty canvas adds selector_3f9a1c20 at that spot and its popup opens. tiles answers with the sections of what can be made. The human picks html, the cell is placed at the spot, and the selector deletes itself.

Sources: canvas_agent.ts: the view and its verbs (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/canvas_agent.ts#L164); canvas_agent.ts: wire (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/canvas_agent.ts#L277); layout.ts: rects per theme, hidden (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/layout.ts#L4); cell_menu.ts: ✕ hides, Shift+✕ deletes (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/cell_menu.ts#L5); selector_agent.ts: the selector (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/selector_agent.ts#L4); action_popup.ts: the tiles (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/action_popup.ts#L96); canvas.md: the view’s verbs (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/docs/canvas.md#L1)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › Views of agents

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/

An agent is not tied to a screen. The canvas and the terminal UI each look at an agent’s record and decide what to draw for it. In the canvas the decision is a short, ordered list, and the agent’s own record has the first say.

This page covers how the app **chooses** a view. Writing one (`panel.html`, `view.calls`, `fantastic.send`) is in [A view](/fantastic/foundations/build/view/). The canvas itself, and where cells sit, is the [Canvas](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/) pillar.

#### The agent is the unit; the cell is a view of it

The **host agent** is the real agent, in the kernel. Its record declares how it is shown. A cell on the canvas holds only layout (where, how big) and a `backend_id`, the agent it shows. Placing a cell with just a `backend_id` makes a view of that agent, drawn as its record says.

the record’s view field (shape):

```
view: {kind: terminal | chat | html | …  OR  handler: <any page bundle>,
       bytes | bytes_file,   calls: [verbs…]}
```

`bytes` or `bytes_file` is the body of an `html` view, and `calls` lists the verbs an `html` or `handler` view may call on its agent. An agent has one view.

#### Choosing: record, kind, stub

`viewOf` in `host_views.ts` reads a record and returns the page bundle that draws it. It tries these in order, and the first match wins:

1. The record has a `view`. A `handler` names a page bundle directly. A `kind` names one of the generic renderers: `terminal`, `chat`, `html`, `mcp`, `resources`, `tasks`, `store`, `scheduler`, `cabinets` or `credentials`. A `view` with no `kind` or `handler`, or with an unknown `kind`, gets the stub.
2. The record has no `view`, and its `handler_module` is `exec_bridge.tools`: a terminal. For `mcp_client.tools`: the MCP view.
3. Its `handler_module` is one of the agentic stores: `agentic_resources`, `task_registry`, `ram_store`, `sqlite_store`, `scheduler` or `credential_store`. Each has its own read-only view. A `cabinet` gets one only when its `cabinet_role` is `manager`.
4. The record has a `memory_store_id` and a `handler_module`, which is what makes an AI agent: a chat.
5. Anything else gets the **stub**: a reflect card.

*Animation: Record, kind, stub* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/choose.mp4). Three host agents. py_ab12 has view {kind: html} in its record, so its own view draws it. runner has no view and is an exec_bridge, so it gets a terminal. notes has neither, so it gets the reflect card.

The stub is `reflect_view`. It shows the agent’s `handler_module`, its sentence, its verbs as the kernel’s `docs` lists them, and the rest of its reflect as JSON. An agent nobody wrote a view for is therefore still visible and documented.

The sidebar uses the same card to open any agent that no other cell shows. Its ✕ hides the card, and Shift+✕ deletes the agent. The card fronts the agent and does not own it.

#### An agent’s own view

A record with `view: {kind: html, …}` is drawn by `agent_view`. The body is the agent’s own small renderer. It comes from the bundle’s view file, `view.bytes_file`, read from `.fantastic/bundles/<handler_module>/` through the host’s `bundles_watch` bridge, with `{{agent}}` replaced by the instance id. Without a file, the record’s inline `view.bytes` is used. With neither, the cell says the agent declares no view body.

The body runs in the same sandboxed panel as an `html` cell, and its calls go out as the cell. A bundle declares the view once, in `bundle.yaml`, and every instance gets it. Editing the view file writes each instance’s `view` again, and its cell re-renders without a restart. A chat card mounts the same panel inside its frame.

the starter python agent’s view (bundle.yaml):

```
view: {kind: html, bytes_file: panel.html, calls: [hello, count, watch]}
```

The `agent_view` cell answers no verbs of its own beyond the panel’s relay. Anything else is refused as `unhandled`, and the hint points at the host agent’s `view` instead.

#### The cell’s grant comes from the view

A cell is an agent too, so the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) judges what it sends. Nobody writes that grant by hand. `cellGrant` derives it as `{<agent id>: [the view’s calls]}` when the cell is placed.

Each generic renderer carries its own fixed list. The stub gets `reflect` (and `docs` on the kernel). A terminal gets `watch`, `status`, `start`, `write`, `ack`, `resize`, `output` and `paste_image`. A chat gets `watch`, `reflect`, `history`, `status`, `send` and `stop`. For an `html` or `handler` view the list is the record’s `calls`, and `watch` is always added, so a view receives its agent’s events.

The read-only views (resources, tasks, store, scheduler, cabinets, credentials) are granted reads and `watch` and no write verb. The credentials view never gets `get`: it shows a name and a grant, not a value. See the [credential store](/fantastic/foundations/agents/credential-store/).

*Animation: The view’s calls become the cell’s grant* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/grant.mp4). py_ab12 declares calls [hello, count]. The canvas adds watch and writes the cell’s can_call as {py_ab12: [hello, count, watch]}. The panel’s hello passes the call gate as the cell. A stop is not in the grant and is refused.

#### The terminal UI: a panel per handler_module

The terminal UI (TUI) decides the same way, with a different key. Selecting an agent in the tree changes the right pane to that agent’s panel. `PanelKind::of` picks it from the agent’s `handler_module`, read from the tree’s reflect.

| handler_module | panel |
|---|---|
| `*_backend.tools`, `ai_core.tools` | AI: conversation |
| `exec_bridge.tools`, only for the shell’s own id `term` | terminal |
| `file_bridge.tools` | files |
| `agentic_resources`, `task_registry`, `ram_store`, `sqlite_store`, `scheduler`, `cabinet`, `credential_store` | read-only panels |
| anything else | generic |

AI agents match by suffix, so a new provider needs no change. A terminal is matched by id as well, because only the shell knows which exec agent it drew as its PTY. Any other `exec_bridge` agent gets the generic panel, which differs from the canvas, where every exec agent is a terminal.

An unknown module is not an error and not a blank pane. The **generic panel** shows the agent’s id, whether it is open or sealed, its sentence, the last call, its egress (`can_call`) and ingress (`callable_by`), its verbs and its rows, and lets you call any declared verb. Its answer, a refusal included, is shown verbatim. A transport leg has only a reflect, so it lands here too.

*Animation: A panel per handler_module* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/tui.mp4). Four agents selected in the tree. A vllm_backend.tools agent gets the AI panel, the shell’s term gets the terminal, another exec_bridge agent gets the generic panel, and so does a module the shell has never seen.

In the public code, `make` in `panel/mod.rs` is a fixed `match` over these kinds. This page therefore claims no plug-in hook for a custom TUI panel: a new handler gets the generic panel.

Sources: host_views.ts: viewOf and cellGrant (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/host_views.ts#L83); agent_view.ts: an agent’s own view (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/agent_view/agent_view.ts#L57); reflect_view.ts: the stub (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/reflect_view/reflect_view.ts#L39); canvas_agent.ts: hostViewCell and place (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/canvas_agent.ts#L27); bundle.yaml of the starter python agent (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/bundle.yaml#L9); panel/mod.rs: PanelKind::of (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/panel/mod.rs#L78); panel/generic.rs: the generic panel (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/panel/generic.rs#L1)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › HTML and GL agents

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/html-gl/

Two kinds of cell on a canvas hold content instead of fronting a host agent. An **html agent** holds the body of a web page. A **gl agent** holds the source of a WebGL scene. Both are ordinary agents with a record, verbs and a `can_call`.

They are page-side TypeScript: they run in the browser’s kernel, and the code says each was ported from a host Python bundle that no longer exists. So this page describes one implementation, with no Rust or Python twin.

#### An html agent holds a body

The handler module is `html_agent.ts`. The body is a string in the agent’s `meta.html`. `get_html` returns `{id, html}`, and `set_html` replaces the body. A cell answers `get_html` and `set_html` (`render_html` is a second name for `get_html`), plus the three `panel_*` relay verbs the panel’s own calls use; any other verb is refused with `unhandled` and a hint that placing, moving and wiring cells are the view’s verbs.

A view creates the cell with `place {kind: "html", …}` and changes it with `update {id, bytes}`; the view itself is on [Views of agents](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/). `set_html` takes the markup as `bytes`, verbatim. After it stores the body, the agent emits `{"type": "reload_html"}` on itself, and the cell’s panel draws the new body in place.

A **page bundle** is a folder under the canvas’s `bundles/` whose `bundle.yaml` has `base: html_agent`, a `sentence` and an `html:` body. Every instance starts with that body until it gets its own from `set_html`. This is the page kind of folder bundle on [Bundles](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/#folder-bundles).

*Animation: set_html: refused, then accepted* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/html-gl/html_set.mp4). The view places cell panel1. A set_html whose body is plain text with no element is refused as bad_arg and the cell keeps its old body. A set_html with a button and a script is stored in meta.html, the agent emits reload_html, and the panel draws the new body.

#### What counts as a body

Before it writes a body, `set_html` checks the shapes that never render a panel. It refuses a body that is empty, has no element (it reads as text), opens a `<script>`, `<style>` or `<textarea>` and never closes it, or ends inside a tag. The last two are what a truncated body looks like. The page bundle’s own `html:` gets the same check when the bundle loads.

the refusal (the reason after the dash varies):

```
{"error": "html_agent: the html body is not html — it is empty", "reason": "bad_arg", "arg": "bytes", "hint": "send the panel's WHOLE markup as <bytes>…</bytes> — verbatim, nothing elided"}
```

A refusal is data, so the AI that wrote the body reads it and sends the whole markup again ([Refusals](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/refusals/)). A reply that passes is `{ok: true, bytes: N}`, possibly with the grant hint below.

#### The sandbox and the connector

The panel draws the body in an `iframe` whose `srcdoc` is a small document: a `<script>` with the connector in `<head>`, then the body. The frame has `sandbox="allow-scripts"`, so it runs scripts with a null origin. If the agent’s record has `trusted: true`, the frame has no sandbox and shares the page’s origin. The code reserves that for the operator’s own content.

The connector defines `fantastic` in the frame, and its only channel to the outside is `postMessage` to the page.

| call | what it does |
|---|---|
| `await fantastic.send(target, payload)` | one send; resolves with the reply |
| `fantastic.emit(target, payload)` | an event into the target’s inbox; no reply |
| `fantastic.watch(src, cb)` | events of `src`; returns a function that stops it |
| `fantastic.onMessage(cb)` | messages sent to this cell |
| `fantastic.openCanvas(id)` | the page loads that canvas |

The page relays each call to the kernel as the cell’s own agent, not as the operator. A `send` reaches the kernel through the cell’s `panel_send`, so the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) judges it: the cell’s `can_call` and the target’s `callable_by` must both name the verb. An `emit` needs `emit` in the cell’s `can_call`, and a target on the page’s kernel must also name it in `callable_by`. A `watch` is gated too, and a refused one comes back to the frame as an event holding the refusal, so it does not look like a subscription that works.

*Animation: The frame calls out through the cell* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/html-gl/connector.mp4). Inside the sandboxed frame of cell panel1, fantastic.send("runner", start) posts a message to the page. The page relays it as panel1 through the call gate. Panel1’s can_call names runner, so the reply returns to the frame. A second send to store is not named, so the gate refuses it.

#### The grant hint

A refused call inside a panel never reaches the AI that wrote it. So the write that sets the body says what is missing. It scans the body for `fantastic.send`, `fantastic.watch` and `fantastic.emit` calls with a literal target. For a `send` with `type: "name"` written inline it records that verb; otherwise it records `*`. It compares the result with the cell’s `can_call`.

set_html reply with a hint (illustrative ids):

```
{"ok": true, "bytes": 212, "grants_missing": {"runner": ["start", "watch"]}, "hint": "this cell's html calls runner but its can_call does not name it — those calls will be refused. Grant it from the view: update {id: …, fields: {can_call: …}}"}
```

The hint only reads the body. It never writes a grant. The grant is a separate write on the view: `update` with `can_call`, or `wire {sender, receiver, verbs}`, which adds the verbs to the sender’s `can_call` and the receiver’s `callable_by`. The view’s `place` and `update` replies carry the same hint.

#### A gl agent holds a scene

The handler module is `gl_agent.ts`. The source is a string of JavaScript in `meta.gl_source`. `get_gl_view` returns `{id, source}`, and `set_gl_source {source}` stores a new source and emits `reload_html` on the agent. It has no html check and no grant hint.

The canvas draws all GL cells into **one shared THREE renderer, scene and camera**, which follow the canvas’s pan and zoom. For a member that is not a view bundle, the canvas calls `get_gl_view`. If a source comes back, it installs it into the GL host, which makes one `THREE.Group` for that cell.

The host compiles the source with `new Function("THREE", "scene", "t", "onFrame", "cleanup", source)`. Here `scene` is the cell’s own group. Unlike an html panel, the source runs in the page itself, not in a frame. The source adds objects to its group and registers behaviour:

- Without `hz`, `onFrame(cb)` runs `cb(time)` on every frame and every frame is drawn. With `{hz}`, the callback makes a frame due at most `hz` times a second; it also runs on any frame drawn for another reason (a pan, a zoom, another cell). A frame with nothing due is not drawn.
- `t.emit(target, payload)` goes out as the cell’s agent, gated by its `can_call` and the target’s `callable_by`, and is dropped when denied. `t.onMessage(cb)` receives what is emitted to the cell. `t.agent_id` is the cell’s id.
- `cleanup` is an array; functions pushed on it run when the view is torn down.

When a view is replaced, the host runs its cleanup functions, removes its group and disposes its geometries, materials and textures. It then mounts the new source in the same place. What triggers this is the host’s `updateView`, which refetches `get_gl_view` and swaps that cell’s group; `set_gl_source` only stores the source and emits `reload_html`. Sibling views are untouched. A source that throws while mounting is logged and removed, and the other views keep drawing. With no GL view left, the render loop stops.

*Animation: GL cells share one scene* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/html-gl/gl_scene.mp4). The canvas calls get_gl_view on cell gl1 and gets a source. The GL host makes a group for gl1 inside the shared scene and runs the source with scene, t, onFrame and cleanup. A second cell gl2 gets its own group. When the host updates gl1, its cleanup runs, its group is replaced, and gl2 keeps drawing.

A GL source is not sandboxed. `t` also carries the page’s host link (`call`, `subscribeState`), which is not gated by the cell’s `can_call`. Only `t.emit` and `onMessage` are the cell’s own. Treat a GL source as page code.

Sources: html_agent: get_html, set_html, page bundles (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/html_agent/html_agent.ts#L31); the html check and its refusal (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/html_check.ts#L11); the connector injected into the frame (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/html_agent/connector.ts#L40); html_view: sandbox, srcdoc and the postMessage relay (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/html_agent/html_view.ts#L50); panel_send, panel_emit, panel_watch (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/panel_relay.ts#L17); the grant hint (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/html_agent/grant_hint.ts#L9); gl_agent: get_gl_view, set_gl_source (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/gl_agent/gl_agent.ts#L14); the GL host: shared scene, mountSource, teardown (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/gl_host.ts#L171)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › Skin and backgrounds

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/skin/

How the canvas looks is not a setting file. It is state on agents, and an AI cell or a person changes it with the same send they use for everything else.

The code keeps three things apart. A **skin** is how everything is coloured and shaped. A **theme** is where the cells sit. A **background** is the picture behind the cells. This page covers the skin and the background and shows where the theme fits.

#### Three things, three agents

Each of the three has its own agent on the page, and none of them moves the others. The page-side agents are TypeScript, packed into the binary with the canvas; the code has no Rust or Python twin for them. Their verbs are reached like any other, through the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/).

|  | answers | lives on | state |
|---|---|---|---|
| skin | colours, radii, fonts, shadows, motion, and the backdrop | the `skin` agent | `skins`, `user_skins` |
| theme | where the cells sit: `free` or `column` | the canvas theme agent, `layout_<theme>` agents | `user_themes`, `hidden_themes` |
| background | one GL scene behind every cell | the view’s `background` agent | `bg_source` |

The docs say it directly: a skin “never moves a cell”. The theme, by contrast, changes the cells’ rectangles and never an agent. The [Canvas](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/) article covers cell placement.

*Animation: Skin, theme, background* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/skin/three.mp4). Three cards, three agents. The skin agent holds design tokens and a backdrop. The canvas theme agent holds themes: where the cells sit, free or column. The view’s background agent holds one GL source. A change to one leaves the other two as they were.

#### The skin: design tokens in a record

A skin is a document of **design tokens** in a subset of the W3C Design Tokens format (2025.10), plus a **backdrop**, `web` or `native`. The `skin` agent is one per canvas, a delete-locked child of the page root, made when missing. Its record holds two fields:

- `skins`: `{web, native}`, the name of the skin used on each backdrop. The defaults are the stock skins `dark` (web) and `glass` (native).
- `user_skins`: `[{name, base, note, tokens}]`, skins written by an AI or a human. `tokens` is a partial document merged over `base`, which is a stock skin or another user skin.

The skin in use is the slot for this tab’s backdrop. A plain browser tab has no shell flag, so it is always `web`. One canvas can therefore show `glass` in the app’s window and `dark` in a browser tab at the same time.

The agent answers six verbs.

| verb | what it does |
|---|---|
| `list` | stock skins, your skins, the two slots, this tab’s backdrop and `in_use` |
| `get {name}` | the tokens as authored, and `merged`, the full document that compiles |
| `schema` | the format, supported and refused features, and every token with its type and CSS name |
| `use {name, backdrop?}` | sets a slot, by default this tab’s |
| `add {name, base, tokens, note?}` | adds or replaces one of yours |
| `delete {name}` | removes one of yours |

#### Writing a skin

A new look is one `add` and one `use`. The `add` carries only what changes; the rest comes from `base`. A token you give replaces the base’s whole token, and groups merge deeply.

the skin agent’s own example (shortened):

```
add {name: "ocean", base: "dark", tokens: {color: {accent: {base: {$value:
  {colorSpace: "srgb", components: [0.2, 0.7, 0.9]}}}}}}
use {name: "ocean"}
```

Before it stores anything, `add` checks the name (1 to 40 characters of `a-z`, `0-9`, `_`, `-`), that it is not a stock name, that `base` exists and has no cycle, and that the merged document compiles. A bad token is refused with its path. The same name replaces the old skin, and if it is in use the page shows the new version at once.

A colour is `srgb` with `components` in 0 to 1, an optional `alpha`, and an optional `hex` that must equal the components. Tokens marked `opaque` must have alpha 1, because the canvas mixes them with its `tint()` helper. Aliases such as `"{color.accent.base}"` are followed, and a `palette.*` group holds free alias targets that are never compiled.

The format refuses `$ref`, `$extends`, `$root`, the types `strokeStyle`, `border`, `transition`, `gradient` and `typography`, and any colour space other than `srgb`.

*Animation: Add a skin, use it* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/skin/skin.mp4). The skin agent receives add with name ocean, base dark and one accent token. The merged document compiles, so ocean is stored. use ocean sets the web slot, and the single fantastic-skin stylesheet is replaced. A native skin sent to the web slot is refused with bad_arg.

#### How the page applies it

The page compiles a skin to one CSS custom property per token, named `--fc-` plus the path with dots as dashes. All of them sit in one `<style id="fantastic-skin">` at the start of the head, and `<html>` gets `data-skin` and `data-backdrop`. Switching skins replaces that stylesheet’s text and the browser restyles every view from the new variables, and the canvas also redraws the view (a native backdrop hides the background).

The page watches the `skin` record and applies again whenever `skins` or `user_skins` changes, so a send from anywhere shows at once. A skin that cannot apply is logged and shown as a toast, and the page keeps the skin it shows.

`use` refuses a skin whose backdrop is `native` for the `web` slot, as `bad_arg`, because nothing is behind a browser tab. A web skin may sit in the `native` slot. `delete` refuses a skin that is in a slot or is another skin’s base.

Font sizes, weights, line heights and layout geometry are not tokens. The docs keep them literal so that a skin never moves a cell.

#### The background: a GL source on its own agent

Every view has exactly one **background** agent, a child of the view. The root view’s is `background` and is delete-locked, so it can only be updated; a nested view’s is `<view>_bg`. Its one piece of state is `bg_source`.

`bg_source` is JavaScript, run as `new Function("THREE", "scene", "t", "onFrame", "cleanup", bytes)` in the page’s shared three.js scene, behind every cell. The agent answers `set_bg {bytes}`, `default_bg`, `clear_bg` and `get_bg`, and `set_bg` refuses a source that does not compile, with the error and `reason` `bad_arg`. The record grants these verbs by name to the view (its parent) and to the backgrounds agent; no one else may call them.

People and AI cells rarely call that agent directly. The page’s **backgrounds agent** (file `backgrounds_agent.ts`, called the canvas theme agent in its own header) manages a list and applies a choice by calling `set_bg` on the view’s background.

- Stock backgrounds are Isoline, Glyph, Copper and Moire. `delete` hides a stock one and `restore_stock` brings all back.
- `add {name, note?, bytes}` adds your own as a full GL source. `add {name, note?, body, sets?}` writes only a body on the stock prelude. Either must compile.
- `set {name, set?}` applies one, `random` picks one, `none` clears, and `default` restores Isoline in its Ember colour set.
- `rotate {on, every_s?}` picks a random one every `every_s` seconds. The default is 60, and values under 5 fall back to it.

Its record keeps `user_bgs`, `hidden_stock`, `current` and `rotate`, so the choice survives a reload. The agent is granted `set_bg`, `clear_bg`, `default_bg` and `get_bg` on the background at both ends, as the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) requires.

*Animation: Set a background* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/skin/background.mp4). The backgrounds agent receives set with the name Isoline. It sends set_bg with the GL source to the view’s background agent, which checks that the source compiles and stores it as bg_source. A source that does not compile is refused with bad_arg. Under a native skin the background is not drawn.

Under a `native` skin the page draws no background, because the window’s own material shows through. The background’s record is untouched, so a web skin brings it back. A skin change also redraws the view.

#### Where the theme fits

The canvas theme agent also keeps the themes, and they are a different thing from a skin. A theme is `{name, layout, trigger}`, where `layout` is `free` or `column`. The stock themes are `canvas` (free) and `mobile` (one column, for tabs under 768 px wide).

With the view’s `theme` set to `auto`, the page takes the first theme whose width trigger matches the tab, yours first, otherwise the first without a trigger. The verbs are `themes`, `use_theme`, `add_theme`, `delete_theme` and `restore_themes`; the stock `canvas` cannot be deleted or hidden; edit it with `add_theme`.

Positions live in one `layout_<theme>` agent per theme under the view. Switching theme moves the cells and never the agents. The [Canvas](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/) article follows from there.

Sources: the skin agent: verbs, record, refusals (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/skin/skin_agent.ts#L128); applying a skin: one style element (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/skin/apply.ts#L13); the token format and what it refuses (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/skin/tokens.ts#L67); the token schema (every token) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/skin/schema.ts#L26); the background agent (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/background_agent.ts#L50); the backgrounds agent (and themes) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/backgrounds/backgrounds_agent.ts#L96); themes and layouts (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/layout.ts#L63); docs: skins (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/docs/skins.md)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › Cabinet

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/cabinet/

A **cabinet** is a canvas of its own with one worker AI. A master AI splits a job into cabinets, gives each worker a task, and reads their reports as they come in.

The `cabinet` bundle holds the rules: which canvas each cabinet gets, what each worker may call, and how the cabinets are removed. The Python bundle is the reference; the Rust bundle is a port with the same verbs, refusals and grants.

#### The parts

One **manager** is a `cabinet.tools` agent with `cabinet_role: manager`. The operator makes it once. It names the canvas that spawns the cabinets in its `canvas_id` field, and the cabinets are its children.

Each cabinet is a record with `cabinet_role: cabinet`. It is the live status cell that the spawning canvas can show, and it owns one worker AI as its child. The cabinet also points at its own canvas, made by `new_canvas`. That canvas is a child of the spawning canvas, as described in [Canvas](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/canvas/).

Deleting a canvas deletes the canvases it spawned. This is what lets a cabinet take its canvas with it when it closes.

- manager verbs: `open_cabinet`, `close_cabinet`, `cabinets`, `conclude`, `reflect`
- cabinet verbs: `status`, `view`, `reflect`

The master is the AI that sends `open_cabinet`. An operator send is refused, because there is no master to wire the cabinet to.

#### Opening a cabinet

The master sends `open_cabinet {task, name?, backend?, setup?}` to the manager. Only `task` is required. The manager then works in this order:

1. It grants itself `new_canvas` on the spawning canvas, and the canvas grants it back.
2. It sends `new_canvas {name}` to the spawning canvas. The new canvas is a child of it.
3. It creates the cabinet record `cabinet_<name>` with its task, its master, its canvas and an empty status.
4. It creates the worker `cabinet_<name>_worker` under the cabinet.
5. It wires the grants described below and rewrites every worker’s directory.

The cabinet and worker records are made by sends to the root as the manager itself, so the operator must grant the manager `create_agent`, `update_agent` and `delete_agent` on the root. See the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/). If any wiring step fails, the manager removes the half-made cabinet and its canvas.

the reply of open_cabinet (illustrative values):

```
{"id": "cabinet_alpha", "canvas": "canvas_cabinet_alpha",
 "worker": "cabinet_alpha_worker", "master": "…",
 "backend": "…", "new_backend": false, "peers": []}
```

The reply does not mean the worker has started. `open_cabinet` does not start the worker. The master sends it the task as its first message, `{type: "send", text: …}`.

*Animation: open_cabinet: a canvas and a worker* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/cabinet/open.mp4). The master sends open_cabinet {task} to the manager. The manager asks the spawning canvas for new_canvas and gets a child canvas. It then creates the cabinet cell and, under it, the worker. The reply names the ids, and the worker waits for its first message.

#### Where the worker comes from

The worker is a copy of an existing AI backend’s record. By default the backend is the master itself, and `backend` names another. The copy keeps the handler, endpoint, model, credential reference and memory store, so the connection and key stay where their owner set them. The record’s identity, grants, prompts, view and cabinet fields are not copied.

`setup` overrides fields of the copy, but a wiring key in it is refused. A worker whose handler, endpoint or credentials differ from the backend’s is flagged `new_backend: true` with a warning. The code allows it and discourages it.

The manager’s optional `max_cabinets` is a ceiling. An open that would exceed it is refused with `reason: "ceiling"`.

#### Who may call whom

Every open edits grants key by key. The pattern follows the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/): each edge needs both a `can_call` and a `callable_by`.

| edge | verbs |
|---|---|
| worker to its cabinet | `status` |
| worker to its cabinet’s canvas | `create`, `place` |
| worker to a peer worker, or to the master | `send`, `reflect` |
| master or manager to a worker | all verbs |
| master to a cabinet | `view`, `reflect` |
| worker to the root | nothing |

> a peer that may only message cannot stop, clear or re-task the other. (cabinet/tools.py)

The worker also holds its memory store, and its credential store when the backend names one. It holds no grant on the root, so it cannot edit grants, and it cannot place a child canvas, because `new_canvas` is not on its grant. When a cabinet closes, the kernel prunes every grant that names a deleted id.

#### The directory

Each live worker’s record carries `cabinet_peers`: the cabinet, worker and task of every other cabinet. Its `post_system_prompt` says it is one of N workers, lists the peers, and shows how to message a peer or the master, how to report `status`, and how to build on its canvas. The text rides after the backend’s own prompt and never replaces it. Both are rewritten on every open and close.

*Animation: Grants between workers* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/cabinet/wiring.mp4). Two cabinets, alpha and beta, each with a worker. The workers get send and reflect grants both ways. The master calls each worker in full. No worker holds any grant on the root.

`open_cabinet`, `close_cabinet` and `conclude` run one at a time per manager. Each reads whole grant maps and writes them back, so two in flight would overwrite each other’s entries. Other verbs are not serialised.

#### What a worker does

A worker builds its **equipment** on its cabinet’s canvas. It sends `create {record: {handler_module, …}}` to build an agent there, for example an exec runner or a helper AI, and `place` to show a view. These are the only two verbs it holds on the canvas. Equipment is a child of the canvas, not of the worker.

The worker reports up with `status {line, progress?, result?}` to its cabinet. `line` is a string, `progress` is a number from 0 to 100, and `result` can hold the final answer. The cabinet stores the report with a timestamp and emits an `update` event on its own id, so its view and every watcher see it live.

status (illustrative values):

```
{"type": "status", "line": "parsing", "progress": 40}
```

The master reads the state in two ways. `cabinets` lists every live cabinet with its task, worker, canvas, status and equipment. `view` on one cabinet returns the same fields for it.

The status cell appears on the spawning canvas once the master places it there with the canvas view’s `place {backend_id: <cabinet>, x, y}`. Its button calls `fantastic.openCanvas(canvas)` and the page switches to the cabinet’s canvas. The button stays disabled until a canvas is named. The Rust terminal panel for a cabinet is read-only and sends only `cabinets` and `view`.

#### Closing and keeping

`close_cabinet {id}` deletes the cabinet with its worker, then its canvas with all the equipment on it, then rewrites the remaining workers’ directories. It refuses an id that is not a cabinet of this manager.

`conclude {keep?}` closes every cabinet that is not named in `keep`, and the manager stays. A `keep` id is either a live cabinet, which stays whole, or a **result**: an agent placed on a cabinet’s canvas at any depth. For a result, the canvas and the path down to it stay. The cabinet record, the worker and all other equipment are deleted.

Any other id is refused with `reason: "unknown_keep"` before anything is deleted. A canvas’s page loader is its own records: it is never deleted and never counts as a result.

*Animation: conclude keeps a result* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/cabinet/conclude.mp4). A worker reports status up to its cabinet. The master sends conclude {keep: ["report"]}, where report sits on a cabinet’s canvas. The canvas and the report stay; the cabinet, the worker and the other equipment are deleted.

#### What the code leaves open

- Equipment is not wired for the worker. A created helper AI gets its memory store and nothing else; the worker reaches other equipment only when its own `can_call`, or a peer’s, names it.
- How many cabinets to open, and what each worker builds, is the model’s choice. The code limits only the ceiling and the grants.

Sources: Python cabinet bundle (reference) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/ai/cabinet/src/cabinet/tools.py#L349); cabinet readme (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/ai/cabinet/src/cabinet/readme.md#L1); status cell (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/ai/cabinet/src/cabinet/view.html#L1); Rust cabinet bundle (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-cabinet/src/lib.rs#L1); new_canvas and the canvas tree (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/web.rs#L8); terminal panel (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/panel/cabinet.rs#L1); the manager view (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/cabinets_view/cabinets_view.ts#L1)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › Web MCP

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/web-mcp/

A coding CLI or any other MCP client can drive a fantastic kernel through two tools, `reflect` and `send`. The part of the kernel that answers it is an agent called the **MCP leg**, with the handler `web_mcp.tools`.

The wire format, the attach-or-run rule and the grants are already in [Transports](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/transports/#mcp). This page goes one layer down: how the leg splits protocol from identity, the config file it keeps, the questions it holds for the person, and the `fantastic send` command.

#### Two layers: the agent and the protocol

The leg lives in the `fantastic-web-mcp` crate, outside the kernel tree. It keeps two things apart on purpose. `WebMcpBundle` is the **agent**: it answers verbs sent to the leg. `McpCore` is the **protocol**: one JSON-RPC message in, one reply out. Every carrier calls `McpCore`, and no carrier knows what MCP means.

The only carrier on `main` is a stream of JSON lines, over stdio or over the kernel’s local socket. The code comments name an HTTP carrier as later, so this page describes none. `McpCore` answers `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list` and `tools/call`, and answers any other method with the error “Method not found”. A notification gets no reply. Protocol version 2025-11-25.

#### A tool call is the leg’s task

A carrier runs outside every dispatch, so anything it sent itself would count as the operator’s. `McpCore` avoids that. It starts a kernel task owned by the leg, and the task sends the leg an `inbound_send` verb with the batch. The leg then sends each item onward as itself, so the leg’s own grants decide every call, as in [Call gate and grants](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/).

*Animation: A tool call becomes the leg’s task* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/web-mcp/two_layers.mp4). A client sends tools/call send to McpCore. McpCore starts a task owned by the mcp leg (task 7, illustrative), which ps lists. The task hands the batch to the leg’s inbound_send. The leg sends the item to files as itself, so its grants decide. When the task ends, the outcomes return as [{pid, status, result}].

The task id exists from the first instant, so `ps` lists the call and `cancel` on it kills the subtree. The client’s `notifications/cancelled` does the same, and an item `timeout` cancels just that item. There is no wait bound: the reply is the outcome whenever the task ends. [Tasks](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/) explains the task table.

#### The two tools

There is no tool per agent or per verb. `reflect` with no arguments reflects `kernel` with `tree` and `bundles` as ids and the readme index on; with a `target` it reflects that agent, and extra arguments pass through. `send` takes `{items: [{target, payload, timeout?}]}`. Each item needs a `target` and a `payload` object whose `type` names the verb.

what send returns (shape):

```
[{"pid": 8, "status": "completed", "result": …}]
```

The result is pretty-printed JSON text, plus `structuredContent` when it is an object. `isError` is true only when nothing in the batch completed. A mixed batch, or a refusal inside one, is data. A shape error in an item, such as a missing `payload.type`, comes back as a tool error naming the item.

#### The mcp agent and how it connects

The agent is named `mcp`. The CLI creates it in code at boot, or on the first connection if it is missing, as a child of the `user` agent, with the handler `web_mcp.tools`. If an agent called `mcp` already runs another handler, the CLI stops with an error and asks you to rename or delete it.

The CLI also grants it every verb on every agent, both edges, except cabinet-owned agents (they keep the grants `fantastic_cabinet` writes for them), and the human reshapes those grants with `update_agent`. [Transports](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/transports/#mcp) describes `fantastic mcp` attaching to a running kernel over `.fantastic/cli/mcp.sock`, or running the kernel itself when none holds the directory’s lock. When it runs the kernel, stdout belongs to the protocol: the real stdout is duplicated to a private descriptor and the log takes over fds 1 and 2.

A `reflect` of the leg shows its sentence, the protocol, the two tools, how many inquiries are open, and `mcp_config_error` when the config check below failed. The leg has no other verbs for a client. A verb it does not know gets `{error, reason: "unhandled"}` with the note that the leg is driven by its carrier.

#### The project’s MCP config

A coding CLI needs to find this kernel. So the leg keeps a file right: `.fantastic/.mcp.json`. At every boot the CLI makes a writable `file_bridge` named `mcp_config`, rooted at the project and exposing only that one file, and names it on the leg as `file_bridge_id` with `mcp_config_file`. The bridge is never rooted at `.fantastic`, because the kernel persists its own records there.

On its boot the leg then reads the file through the bridge, as itself, with `read_stream`. It sets `mcpServers.fantastic` to `{command: <this binary, absolute path>, args: ["mcp"]}`, and writes the file back with `write` only when that entry changed. A missing file counts as `{}`. Every other server and key keeps its place, so a moved or rebuilt binary is corrected on the next start.

*Animation: The leg keeps .mcp.json right* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/web-mcp/config_file.mp4). At boot the mcp leg reaches .fantastic/.mcp.json through its mcp_config bridge. It reads the file with read_stream and keeps the other servers. It sets mcpServers.fantastic to this binary with args mcp, and writes with write only if the entry changed. A bad file or a missing grant makes the boot answer with reason mcp_config.

A failure is loud and nothing is overwritten. The boot answers `{error, reason: "mcp_config"}` and the leg’s `reflect` carries `mcp_config_error` until a boot succeeds. The causes are a bridge named without a file path, a bridge that does not admit the leg, a file that is not a JSON object, and `mcpServers` that is not an object. To use the file, point the client at it: `claude --mcp-config .fantastic/.mcp.json`.

#### Inquiries: questions for the person

Some decisions belong to the human who drives the kernel through the leg. An agent sends the leg `inquiry {text, kind?, options?, request_id?, reply_client_id?}`. The `kind` is `text`, `single`, `multi` or `confirm`, and `single` and `multi` need `options`. The leg accepts at once with `{accepted, re, request_id, open}` and holds the question. `re` is the pid the inquiry runs under, and it is the handle for the answer.

The person lists the open ones with `inquiries`, oldest first, optionally for one `asker`. They answer with `answer {re, text}`, where `text` is words, a list of picks or a boolean. The leg sends the asker a message shaped `[reply to <re> · <leg> inquiry]`, then closes the inquiry. If that send fails, the question stays open and `answer` returns `reason: "refused"`.

*Animation: An inquiry waits for the person* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/web-mcp/inquiry.mp4). An agent sends the mcp leg inquiry with kind confirm. The leg accepts at once with re 12 (illustrative pid) and holds it in open_inquiries. The person lists inquiries and sends answer with re 12 and the text yes. The asker receives [reply to 12 · mcp inquiry] and the inquiry closes.

The open list is durable. It lives on the leg’s own record as `open_inquiries`, written through the kernel’s ordinary update, so an unanswered question is still there after a restart.

#### fantastic send: one call from a shell

`fantastic send '<item json>'` makes one call into the kernel running in the current directory, as the `mcp` leg. It is attach-only: it opens the same socket, speaks `initialize` and one `tools/call` of `send`, and prints the item’s `{pid, status, result}`. With no live kernel it exits 1 and starts nothing. The exit code is 0 only when the item completed.

A payload string value that starts with `$env:`, at any depth, is replaced by the variable of the calling shell named by the rest of the string. This is the only place `$env:` is resolved, and the kernel never reads its own environment for it. A string with text before `$env:` is left alone. An unset variable exits 2 before anything is sent.

storing a key (from the connected client’s instructions):

```
KEY=$(op read op://vault/openai/key) fantastic send '{"target":"credentials","payload":{"type":"set","ref":"responses/api.openai.com","fields":{"api_key":"$env:KEY"}}}'
```

The CLI docs say `send` items also take `secret` marks. In the code the MCP carrier builds each item without reading one, and `fantastic send` substitutes `$env:` without marking a path. This page claims neither. [Credential store](/fantastic/foundations/agents/credential-store/) covers where keys go.

Sources: lib.rs: WebMcpBundle, McpCore, the two tools (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-web-mcp/src/lib.rs#L1); McpCore.run: a tool call as the leg’s task (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-web-mcp/src/lib.rs#L418); the config sync: with_entry and write_config (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-web-mcp/src/lib.rs#L160); inquiries.rs: inquiry, inquiries, answer (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-web-mcp/src/inquiries.rs#L1); mcp.rs: attach or run, the socket, ensure_leg (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/mcp.rs#L1); mcp_config.rs: .fantastic/.mcp.json and its bridge (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/mcp_config.rs#L1); send.rs: fantastic send and $env: (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/send.rs#L1); the crate’s tests (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/tree/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-web-mcp/tests)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › User home store

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/home-store/

A project keeps its agents in its own `.fantastic/` folder. Some choices belong to the person instead, and should follow them from project to project, such as which model an AI agent uses. Fantastic keeps those in the user’s **home**: `FANTASTIC_HOME`, or `~/.fantastic` when it is unset.

This page is about the **saved set-up**: a named blueprint for an agent, kept as one file in the home. It covers what the file may hold, how it is written and protected, and how the canvas makes an AI agent from it. The Rust CLI provides the store; the Python runtime has no twin of it.

#### What the home holds

The `user_home_store.tools` bundle owns one directory of the home. Next to it sit the key refs (see the [credential store](/fantastic/foundations/agents/credential-store/)) and the stored locations of your fantastics.

the layout (opus is an illustrative name):

```
<home>/                         0700
  user/                         0700
    setups/ai_agent/            0700
      opus.yaml                 0600
      .preferred                0600
    keys/                       0700
  fantastics/                   0700
```

The binary fixes the directory when it registers the bundle. Nothing on a record can move it, so a cloned project whose record names the same bundle still gets the same store and cannot point it at another place. If neither `FANTASTIC_HOME` nor the user’s home variable is set, the store has no home, and it says which variable is missing.

Who reaches the store is its `callable_by`, as for every agent. The CLI makes an agent `user_home` under `user` and grants `user` exactly `persist_record`, `forget_record`, `load_tree`, `prefer` and `reflect`. It sets that grant again on every boot, so a record on disk that widened it is narrowed. The [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) refuses every other caller.

#### A blueprint, not an agent

A saved set-up is a `handler_module` plus that bundle’s own settings, such as a model and an endpoint. It is not an agent. It carries no identity, no per-project wiring and no authority. The store refuses a record that holds any of these fields:

fields a saved set-up may never carry:

```
id  parent_id  guid  agents  memory_store_id
can_call  callable_by  ingress_rule  egress_rule  auth
```

The refusal is `invalid_meta`, names the fields to drop, and adds the hint that the creator supplies id, parent, memory store and grants when it makes an agent from the set-up. The store keeps no key values either. A set-up may name a key by its ref (`credentials: {store, ref}`), and the value stays in the credential store.

The record must also be a record the target bundle would accept. The bundle must be linked into this build. Its record schema decides which fields are required and which values an enumerated field may take. A bundle without a schema is checked by its own `validate_meta`. A record that fails the bundle’s schema is refused when saved, not when used. Other problems, such as a handler that is not an AI backend, appear when the canvas makes an agent from it.

*Animation: A blueprint, not an agent* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/home-store/blueprint.mp4). With illustrative names, a record with a handler_module and a model also carries id ai_1 and a can_call grant. persist_record opus is refused with invalid_meta, which says to drop id and can_call. Without them the record passes the bundle’s checks, opus.yaml is written with mode 0600, and the store answers {name, version, path}.

#### Four verbs

| verb | what it does |
|---|---|
| `persist_record {name, record, if_match?}` | checks and writes `<name>.yaml`; answers `{name, version, path}` |
| `forget_record {name, if_match?}` | deletes the file; answers `{name, forgotten}`; clears the default if it was this one |
| `load_tree` | answers `{saved: [{name, version, record}], preferred, dir}`, sorted by name |
| `prefer {name}` | writes the default’s name to `.preferred`; the set-up must exist; `{name: null}` clears it |

A name is letters, digits, `-` and `_`, starts with a letter or digit, and is at most 64 characters, so a name is never a path. A read creates nothing: with no set-ups ever saved, `load_tree` answers an empty list and does not make the home folder.

Nothing is a default until someone calls `prefer`. Deleting the `user_home` agent never deletes the files, because the set-ups belong to the user, not to the project.

#### Private files and lost updates

Directories are created `0700` and files `0600`, with that mode from the start. A write goes to a temporary file that is synced and then renamed over the target, so a reader never sees half a file.

The store applies the ssh rule on every read and write. A set-up file or a directory on the path that is readable or writable by group or others is refused as `unauthorized`, and the refusal names the fix, a `chmod`.

The **version** of a set-up is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its bytes. Two running fantastics share one home, so a save can overwrite a change it never saw. Passing `if_match` with the version you read prevents that: if the file differs, the save is refused and the hint says to `load_tree` again and retry.

a stale save (illustrative versions):

```
persist_record {"name": "opus", "record": {...}, "if_match": "a1b2…"}
→ bad_arg  arg: if_match
  persist_record: opus changed since you read it (you had a1b2…, it is c3d4…)
  hint: load_tree again, then retry
```

*Animation: Two fantastics, one file* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/home-store/guard.mp4). Fantastics A and B both read opus with load_tree and get version a1b2. B saves first through a temp file and a rename, and the version becomes c3d4. A then saves with if_match a1b2, and the store refuses it with bad_arg: the file changed since A read it. The hint says to load_tree again and retry.

#### From a set-up to an AI agent

The canvas uses the store when it makes an AI agent. A `spawn` names a saved set-up, or else uses the preferred one. With neither, it answers `not_found`, “no default AI set-up”, and the hint says to save one and make it the default. A set-up whose handler is not an AI backend, one whose handler’s record schema has no `memory_store_id` field, is refused with `bad_arg` at this point, not when saved.

The store accepts any bundle that is linked in and passes its schema, so this check belongs to the canvas, not to the store. The agent gets the id `ai_<hex>`, made at creation. Its fields come from the set-up plus the stamp its caller supplies, and the creator adds the memory store and the grants.

*Animation: From a set-up to an agent* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/home-store/apply.mp4). The saved set-ups opus and sonnet are listed by load_tree. prefer marks opus as the default. With illustrative names, a spawn that names no set-up reads the preferred one and makes the AI agent ai_3f9a1c02 with the record’s model. Its id, memory store and grants are added at creation.

The CLI’s own set-up flow, the wizard, saves the first set-up as the default when none is set. It also names the stored key for the endpoint, when one is stored, as `credentials` before saving.
