When it makes an agent from a saved set-up, it drops `handler_module` and `credentials` from the record, names the key again for the endpoint, and writes the agent under a free id (`opus`, `opus-2`, and so on).

#### The user store beside it

A second agent, `user_store`, is made under `user` on every boot. It reads the same home and shows what the user keeps: key refs with their hosts, the names of the saved set-ups, and the locations of stored fantastics. Each stored fantastic has a folder `<home>/fantastics/<guid or name>/fantastic.yaml` with its project path, process id and canvas URL. A switch on its record, `register_home_folder`, turns that folder on or off. The canvas places its own view of it from the double-click menu.

Sources: lib.rs: the store, its layout and rules (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user-home-store/src/lib.rs#L1); lib.rs: persist_record (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user-home-store/src/lib.rs#L248); readme.md: the store’s own summary (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user-home-store/src/readme.md#L1); kern/saved.rs: the user_home agent and its grants (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/saved.rs#L1); kern/backend.rs: spawn from a saved set-up (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/backend.rs#L192); kern/wizard.rs: create and from_saved (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/wizard.rs#L59); user_store.rs: the stored fantastics (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user-home-store/src/user_store.rs#L1); tests.rs: the store’s behaviour (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-user-home-store/src/tests.rs#L62)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › Canvas page

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/page/

The canvas is a web page, and the binary that runs the kernel carries it. There is no folder of assets to install and no second server. A **`canvas_page`** agent holds the page and hands it out, one file at a time, to the `web` host.

This page follows the page from build to browser: how it is packed and embedded, what the agent answers, and what the page does in its first moments. What the canvas then draws is the subject of the other Canvas pages. This page covers the Rust runtime. The Python runtime has no `canvas_page` bundle on `main`.

#### Packed at build, embedded in the binary

`canvas_page` is an ordinary [bundle](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/), built outside the kernel tree. Its handler module is `canvas_page.tools`, and it is a child of a `web` host.

Its `build.rs` runs the canvas app’s `scripts/pack.sh`, which needs only a POSIX shell, a vendored esbuild pinned by its sha256, and no npm or node. The result is `canvas.zip`. The build script writes it under `OUT_DIR`, never into the source tree, and the crate embeds it with `include_bytes!`. A failed pack fails the build, because a binary without its page is not a build.

The zip has three entries, in a fixed order: `readme.md`, `bundle.min.js` and `bundle.min.js.map`. `bundle.min.js` is the whole page in one file. The canvas, its views, the TypeScript kernel library, three.js and xterm are all inlined, and the pack refuses a bundle with a bare vendor import left in it.

The zip is reproducible. Every entry gets mode 644, no extra fields and a time taken from `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` (1980-01-01 UTC when unset), so the same inputs give the same bytes whatever the clock, the umask or the time zone. The pack also stamps the sha256 of `bundle.min.js` into the zip’s copy of `readme.md`, as `expected: …`.

*Animation: Packed at build, embedded in the binary* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/page/embed.mp4). build.rs runs pack.sh, which turns the canvas app into canvas.zip with three entries: readme.md, bundle.min.js and bundle.min.js.map. The crate embeds the zip with include_bytes!, so the binary carries the page. A failed pack fails the build.

#### Six files, one agent

The agent inflates the zip once and keeps the files in a map by name. It adds three small pages of its own, so it serves six files.

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | one `<script type="module" src="bundle.min.js">` tag, so the bundle is the whole page; the path is relative, so it loads under whatever id the agent has |
| `home.html` | the same tag with `<body data-page="home">`; the bundle then boots the Home page instead of the canvas |
| `list.html` | the example client of the `home` protocol, a single file with no build step |
| `bundle.min.js`, `bundle.min.js.map`, `readme.md` | the three entries of `canvas.zip` |

The choice between canvas and Home is made inside the bundle. Its entry file imports the Home when `document.body.dataset.page` is `home`, and the canvas for every other page.

The agent holds no state and writes nothing. Its sentence says it serves the files “read-only (transport only)”.

#### Serving it: the web host reads as itself

`canvas_page` answers four verbs:

| verb | answer |
|---|---|
| `reflect` | `id`, a sentence, and `files`, the served names |
| `boot` | a no-op, `{"booted": true}`: the parent `web` host serves the route |
| `list` | `{"files": [...]}` |
| `read_stream {path, offset?, length?}` | a chunk of one file |

Any other verb gets an error with `reason` `unhandled`. `read_stream` is the one that matters. The record declares it in its `verbs`, which is what lets the host’s generic file route, `GET /<id>/file/<path>`, serve this agent. That route is described in [Web agents](/fantastic/foundations/agents/web/#files).

Once the canvas is running, the page lives at `/canvas_page/file/index.html`. The host reads as itself, so the read passes the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) like any send. `fantastic canvas` writes both halves: `web` has `can_call` for `read_stream` on `canvas_page`, and `canvas_page` has `callable_by` for it from `web`.

the head of a read_stream reply:

```
{"path": "index.html", "offset": 0, "next_offset": 10, "eof": false, "size": 173}
```

A reply is a **binary reply**. The bytes are the body, under the key `bytes`, and the head carries `path`, `offset`, `next_offset`, `eof` and `size`. A caller that sends text only gets the head. The host asks for 256 KiB at a time and walks `next_offset` until `eof`.

A path the agent does not have is refused with `reason` `not_found`, and the error lists the files it does serve. The lookup is a map of names, not a filesystem path, so a name like `../secret` is simply not in the map.

*Animation: Serving it: the web host reads as itself* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/page/serve.mp4). A browser asks web for /canvas_page/file/index.html. web sends read_stream to canvas_page as itself, with can_call and callable_by both granting it. canvas_page answers with the bytes and a head. A name it does not hold is refused with not_found.

The home kernel creates the same agent under its own `web` host. It serves `home.html` and `list.html` at `/canvas_page/file/…`, and the desktop app’s window filter admits those URLs.

#### What the page does when it loads

The page is its own kernel, running in the browser, and a peer of the host kernel. It talks to the host over the socket leg `canvas_ws`. Its first steps run in a fixed order:

1. Read the shell flag. A desktop shell sets one frozen global, `window.__FANTASTIC_SHELL__`, with `name`, `os`, `webview`, `backdrop` and an optional `pickFolder`. A plain browser tab has none. A malformed flag is said in place of the page, and nothing else runs.
2. Install the stock skin, so the first paint is already styled.
3. Build the kernel and its bridge. Every host call goes through the host’s `user` agent: a call to agent `T` is sent as `user.forward {target: T, payload}`.
4. Send `reflect` to `kernel` through `user`. If the reply’s `reason` is `unauthorized`, the page shows “The host refused this canvas” with the reason, and stops.
5. List the host’s agents, keep the canvases, and pick one: `?canvas=<id>` if given, else the main one, else the first. An unknown id shows “no canvas <id> on this host”.
6. Load that canvas’s page bundles and page records through its loader, a `kernel_state` agent on the host. An empty tree is seeded with the canvas root. Every later local change is persisted back through the same loader.
7. Boot the root. The first boot mints the page’s guid, and the host addresses the page as `<guid>|canvas`. Then mount the canvas.

*Animation: What the page does when it loads* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/page/boot.mp4). The page kernel sends reflect to kernel through user.forward. An unauthorized reply stops it with a refusal. Otherwise it picks a canvas, loads its records through the loader, boots its root to mint a guid, and mounts the canvas.

The page also watches its own `bundles/` folder on the host through the `bundles_watch` bridge. When a file changes, it waits 150 ms, collects the burst, and sends `reload_bundle` for each touched folder. Nothing runs while nothing changes. When the host stops, it calls `host_stopping` on the page first, and the page flushes its records and stops its loader before the socket closes.

The Home page, `home.html`, boots the same way. It mounts one view onto the host’s `home` agent, and its open pages and selection live in that agent’s state, not in page records.

Sources: canvas_page bundle: verbs, files and read_stream (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-canvas-page/src/lib.rs#L29); build.rs: pack, then embed (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-canvas-page/build.rs#L11); pack.sh: one bundle, vendors inlined (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/scripts/pack.sh#L1); zip_repro.sh: the reproducible zip (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-canvas-page/tests/zip_repro.sh#L1); kern/web.rs: creating the page and both grants (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/web.rs#L308); main.ts: the page’s boot (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/main.ts#L118); user_bridge.ts: every call through user (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/user_bridge.ts#L1); the canvas app (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/tree/main/src/tui/web/canvas)

### Foundations › Canvas: an app built on fantastic › System agents

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/system/

The **system agents** are six agents that stand for the machine itself: `power`, `network`, `audio`, `displays`, `notifications` and `lock`. They are the agents of fantastic OS, and they are Rust only: the code on `main` has no Python twin.

An AI calls them like any other agent: `reflect`, `state`, then their verbs. This page shows how each one is built, what it refuses and why, and why `lock` answers `user` alone.

#### Where they come from

`fantastic system` and `fantastic canvas system` name the **system recipe**. On start, it makes each of the six agents under `user`. If an agent already exists, it updates it instead and resets its view, its `callable_by` and its display name, so a new build’s view replaces the old one.

Each agent gets an html view, which is a canvas cell, and `user` is granted the agent’s verbs. A view only sends to its own agent id.

The recipe is Linux only. Anywhere else it is refused with “`system` needs Linux with D-Bus: the system agents are fantastic OS’s”. For how a canvas shows a view, see [Views](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/).

| agent | handler | the machine side |
|---|---|---|
| `power` | `power.tools` | UPower and logind: battery, lid, power off, reboot, suspend, hibernate |
| `network` | `network.tools` | NetworkManager: devices, Wi-Fi access points, saved connections |
| `audio` | `audio.tools` | PipeWire: `pw-dump` reads, `wpctl` acts |
| `displays` | `displays.tools` | `wlr-randr` for outputs; logind for the backlight |
| `notifications` | `notifications.tools` | the session bus: the agent is the notification server |
| `lock` | `lock.tools` | logind’s session lock and a PIN kept as a hash |

#### Model, driver, port

Every agent is built in three layers. The **ViewModel** is pure: `reduce(event)` is its only mutation and returns **effects** as plain data, and `state()` is what a view draws. Time arrives as a number in an event, and nothing in the model touches the OS.

The **driver** is one task per agent. It feeds events in, runs each effect through the **OS port**, and feeds the answers back. Only the Linux side of the port talks to the machine: D-Bus, `wpctl`, `wlr-randr`. On any other OS the port refuses.

When a reduce changes the state, the driver emits `{"type": "state", "state": …}` to the agent’s watchers. It emits at most once per 100 ms, and always the latest state. A tick reaches each model every 5 seconds, so a model can re-read the machine or expire an item.

A verb’s reply is the state after its effects ran, or the first refusal. A change made elsewhere reaches the watchers too, because the port reports OS-side changes as events. For how watchers receive an emit, see [Records](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/) and [Messages](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/messages/).

*Animation: Model, driver, port* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/system/layers.mp4). A verb reaches the power model as an event. The model returns an effect as data, the driver runs it through the OS port, and the answer comes back as an event. The driver then emits one state to the watchers.

#### Unavailable, and refusals that say why

When a service is missing, the agent still exists. `reflect` and `state` say `available: false` with a `why`, and every other verb is refused with the reason `unavailable`. The boot does not fail.

A refusal is `{error, reason}`, the shape from [Refusals](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/refusals/). The reasons here are these.

| reason | meaning |
|---|---|
| `unavailable` | the service is not there, or a read has not succeeded yet |
| `denied` | the OS asked for authentication or said no |
| `unsupported` | this machine cannot do it, or the verb is not offered in this state |
| `failed` | any other OS error |
| `bad_arg`, `not_found` | a verb’s arguments: missing or wrong, or naming nothing that exists |

The power verbs show the pattern. logind reports `can` for each of `power_off`, `reboot`, `suspend` and `hibernate` as `yes`, `no`, `challenge` or `na`, and the model reads it at start and again every 30 seconds. A verb runs only when its `can` is `yes`.

power: logind’s can decides:

```
yes        -> the call runs
challenge  -> denied: "needs authentication — is the polkit rule installed?"
no, na     -> unsupported: "this machine cannot"
```

The decision is made in the model, before the OS is asked. Nothing in these agents is interactive: there is no authentication prompt. On fantastic OS, a polkit rule lets the user `fantastic` power off, reboot, suspend and hibernate, and use NetworkManager.

*Animation: logind’s can decides* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/system/refusal.mp4). The power agent holds can for each verb. suspend, with can yes, runs and returns the state. reboot, with can challenge, is refused denied. hibernate, with can na, is refused unsupported. The model decides before the OS is asked.

#### What each agent adds

#### network

Verbs: `scan`, `connect {ssid, password?}`, `activate {uuid}`, `deactivate {iface}`, `forget {uuid}` and `set_wireless {enabled}`. `connect` activates a saved connection with that SSID, and otherwise makes a new one. It refuses with `bad_arg` for a missing `ssid`, a missing password or a WPA password that is not 8 to 63 characters or 64 hex digits. It refuses `enterprise` and `wep` networks as `unsupported`, and refuses with `not_found` when the SSID is not in range. The password is held in a type that does not serialize, so it is not in the state.

#### audio

Verbs: `set_volume {volume, id?}`, `set_mute {muted, id?}` and `set_default {id}`. Without `id` they act on the default sink. A volume is clamped to 0.0 to 1.5. The state follows `pw-dump --monitor`, so a change made by another program reaches the watchers.

#### displays

Verbs: `set_output {name, mode?, scale?, transform?, position?, enabled?}` and `set_brightness {value}`. `wlr-randr` has no change stream, so the state is read every 5 seconds and after each verb. Turning off the last enabled output is refused as `unsupported`, because it would leave no screen.

#### notifications

This agent is the session’s notification server: it owns `org.freedesktop.Notifications`, so a notification from any program lands in `state`. The state keeps at most 50 items. The default lifetime is 8 seconds, and the model expires items on its own clock. Verbs: `notify`, `dismiss`, `dismiss_all`, `invoke` and `set_dnd`. With do-not-disturb on, new items still arrive, marked `quiet`.

#### lock: for the person only

The `lock` agent drives the kiosk’s PIN lock screen. The Home page draws the overlay while `state.locked` is true. The code calls it “a kiosk UI lock, not a security boundary”.

Its verbs are `lock`, `unlock {pin}`, `set_pin {new, old?}`, `clear_pin {pin}`, `set_auto_lock {minutes}` and `activity`. A PIN is text of 4 to 12 digits. Nothing locks until a PIN exists: `lock` is refused as `unsupported` with “set a PIN first, or nothing could unlock the screen”.

After the fifth wrong PIN in a row, `retry_at_ms` is set; each try before it is refused `retry_later`. The first wait is 30 seconds, and it doubles up to 15 minutes. While a PIN is being checked, another PIN verb is refused `busy`.

lock state (illustrative values):

```
{"available": true, "locked": true, "has_pin": true,
 "auto_lock_min": 10, "failures": 5, "retry_at_ms": 1760000000000}
```

Unlike the other five, `lock` is not granted to an AI. The recipe’s grant code narrows it: the `callable_by` of `lock` keeps `user` alone, and no AI holder is granted `lock` in its `can_call`. The [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) therefore refuses an AI’s call at the caller’s own end first, so it never reaches `lock`, and no AI can unlock the screen or change the PIN.

*Animation: lock answers user alone* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/canvas/system/lock.mp4). An AI calls lock and the gate refuses it at its own end: no AI holder is granted lock, and lock’s callable_by names user only. The person sends unlock with a wrong PIN five times in a row. After the fifth, each try gets retry_later; the first wait is 30 seconds and it doubles up to 15 minutes.

Sources: The six agents and their ids (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-system-agents/src/lib.rs#L15); The driver: events, effects, 100 ms emit (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-system-agents/src/driver.rs#L1); The OS port and its errors (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-system-agents/src/sys/mod.rs#L15); The recipe that makes them under user (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/system.rs#L19); Power: logind’s can decides (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/crates/fantastic-system/src/power.rs#L225); Lock: PIN, waits, refusals (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/crates/fantastic-system/src/lock.rs#L14); lock is narrowed to user (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/reach.rs#L164); The pure models (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/tree/main/src/tui/crates/fantastic-system/src)

### Foundations › Build your own

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/

Fantastic grows by new kinds of agents. The rule to keep in mind is the one the bundles doc opens with: a **bundle** is code, an **agent** is an instance of it.

#### A bundle and its agents

|  | a bundle | an agent |
|---|---|---|
| what | code: `bundle.yaml` (its verbs), `agent.py`, `panel.html` (its view) | a record that names the bundle |
| where | `.fantastic/bundles/<name>/` | `.fantastic/agents/…/<id>/agent.yaml` |
| one of | per project | many per bundle |

A new verb is a function passed to `fa.serve` and a line in `bundle.yaml` `verbs`; the two must match, or the kernel refuses the agent. Saving `agent.py` restarts every instance; editing `panel.html` re-renders every instance’s cell.

*Animation: One bundle, many agents* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle.mp4). A folder bundle holds bundle.yaml, agent.py and panel.html. Two agents are instances of it, each a record that names the bundle. Saving agent.py restarts both at once; each agent keeps its own record.

Folder bundles are one way in. Below them, a Rust bundle is a crate implementing the kernel’s `Bundle` trait, linked into the binary at build time, and the Python kernel finds its bundles through entry points.

In this part: A bundle (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle/); A program agent (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/program-agent/); A view (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/view/); Example: Team (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/team/)

Sources: README.md: folder bundles (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/README.md#L341); bundles.md (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/docs/bundles.md#L3); the python agent starter (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/agent.py#L1); bundle.rs: the Bundle trait (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/bundle.rs#L50)

### Foundations › Build your own › A bundle

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle/

A bundle is the code behind a `handler_module`. [Kernel › Bundles](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/) explains how the kernel finds one. This page is the how-to: what to write, in Python or in Rust, so that an agent of your bundle answers its verbs.

The examples come from two real bundles that exist in both runtimes. The `scheduler` shows verbs, docs and hooks. The `static_loader` shows a record field and its check. The code blocks that name `tally` are illustrative; the shapes are the real ones.

#### Start from a pair that already exists

The `scheduler` bundle has a Python file and a Rust file that answer the same nine verbs under one `handler_module`, `scheduler.tools`. Read them side by side before you write your own.

|  | Python | Rust |
|---|---|---|
| the code | `bundled_agents/scheduler/src/scheduler/tools.py` | `crates/bundles/fantastic-scheduler/src/lib.rs` |
| how the kernel finds it | an entry point in `pyproject.toml` | `reg.register("scheduler.tools", …)` in the CLI |
| its tests | `tests/test_scheduler.py` | `src/tests.rs` |

Python is the reference. [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) says that when the two disagree, Python is right. The Rust file copies Python’s verb docs and refusal texts, and its comments say so.

*Animation: One bundle, a file in each runtime* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle/twin.mp4). The handler_module scheduler.tools has two implementations. In Python, pyproject.toml publishes the module in the fantastic.bundles group, and tools.py holds VERBS and handler(). In Rust, main.rs calls reg.register, and lib.rs holds impl Bundle with handle(). Both answer to scheduler.tools and serve the same verbs: schedule, list, pause, history and the rest.

#### In Python: a module with a verb table

A Python bundle is a module with an `async def handler(id, payload, agent)`. The kernel awaits it for every verb that is not a kernel verb, and passes the agent object as the third argument. The scheduler calls that parameter `kernel`; it is the agent’s handle for `get`, `update`, `emit` and `send`.

tally/tools.py (illustrative; the scheduler’s handler is this shape):

```
VERBS = {"reflect": _reflect, "bump": _bump}

async def handler(id, payload, agent):
    fn = VERBS.get(payload.get("type"))
    if fn is None:
        return refusal(UNHANDLED, f"tally: unknown type {payload.get('type')!r}",
                       verb=payload.get("type"))
    return await fn(id, payload, agent)
```

Each verb is a function that returns a dict. A refusal comes from `kernel._refusal`: `refusal(UNHANDLED, …, verb=…)` for an unknown verb, and `bad(verb, arg, want)` for an argument that is present but wrong. Both carry a machine `reason`; see [Refusals](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/refusals/).

To make the module reachable, publish it in the `fantastic.bundles` entry-point group. The kernel resolves a `handler_module` only from that catalog, so a module without an entry point answers “No module named”.

pyproject.toml (illustrative; the scheduler publishes scheduler = "scheduler.tools"):

```
[project.entry-points."fantastic.bundles"]
tally = "tally.tools"
```

The package layout is `src/<package>/tools.py`, an optional `readme.md` that the kernel reads from the package, and a `tests/` folder. A module with no entry point can still dispatch in tests through `register_unlisted`.

#### In Rust: a crate that implements Bundle

A Rust bundle is a crate that implements the `Bundle` trait of `fantastic-kernel`. Only two methods are required: `name()` and `handle()`. Every other method has a default that does nothing.

the trait (illustrative; the scheduler implements these):

```
impl Bundle for TallyBundle {
    fn name(&self) -> &str { "tally" }
    fn verb_docs(&self) -> Value { json!({ "bump": "args: by:int?. Returns {count}." }) }
    async fn handle(&self, agent_id: &AgentId, payload: &Value,
                    kernel: &Arc<Kernel>) -> Result<Reply, BundleError> { /* match on payload["type"] */ }
}
```

`handle` matches on `payload["type"]` and returns `Ok(Some(reply))`. `Ok(None)` means no reply. A domain error is a normal reply with an `error` field; `Err` is for a failure of the substrate. The unknown-verb arm builds the same `unhandled` refusal with the `verb` field that Python builds.

The kernel does not load Rust bundles at run time. A crate is linked into the binary, and the host registers it under its `handler_module` string. The CLI does that in `register_default_bundles()`. A host that is not the CLI can register its own bundles after the stock set, with an `Extra` function passed to the TUI shell’s `main_with`; registering a stock name again replaces the stock bundle.

aisixteen/fantastic: fantastic-cli/src/main.rs:

```
reg.register("scheduler.tools", fantastic_scheduler::SchedulerBundle);
```

`fantastic-web-mcp` is a public example of a bundle written outside the kernel tree. Among the workspace crates, its non-test dependencies include only `fantastic-kernel`, and its comment says every API it touches is the kernel’s public surface. In the repository’s own workspace, a crate also needs a line in the workspace `members` and a dependency in the CLI’s `Cargo.toml`.

The scheduler crate also depends on `fantastic-bundle`. That crate holds helpers that format values the way Python does (`repr`, `str`, truthiness), so a Rust refusal text matches Python’s byte for byte. A new bundle needs it only when it must match a Python text exactly.

#### Verbs and their docs

Every verb gets one doc. In Python the doc is the verb function’s docstring, and the `VERBS` table is where the kernel reads them. In Rust it is the map that `verb_docs()` returns, `{verb: doc}`, in the bundle’s order. The scheduler’s Rust map holds the first paragraph of each Python docstring.

The kernel’s `docs` verb serves them. The default tier, `oneliners`, cuts each doc at its first top-level `. ` or ` — `, outside brackets. The `detailed` tier returns the whole doc. Rust’s `docs::signature` mirrors Python’s rule, so write the doc’s first sentence as the signature: the arguments, then what it returns.

a verb doc (the scheduler’s `schedule`, shortened):

```
"schedule": "args: target:str, payload:{type:<verb>, ...}, interval_seconds:int (default 60). ... Returns {schedule_id, schedule}."
```

A bundle can publish more. In Python the module attributes `EMITS`, `CANCEL` and `NOTES` are served by `docs` at the detailed tier; in Rust the methods `emits_doc`, `cancel_doc` and `notes_doc` do the same. The scheduler declares its one event, `schedule_fired`, in `EMITS`.

The docs never ride on a reflect. The scheduler’s own test checks it: a `reflect` of a scheduler carries no `verbs` or `emits`, and `docs` of the same agent lists `schedule` and `schedule_fired`. Keep a verb’s how-to in its doc, and keep `reflect` for what the agent is: the scheduler answers `id`, `sentence`, `paused` and `running`.

*Animation: Verbs and their docs* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle/docs.mp4). The bundle writes one doc per verb, in the VERBS table in Python or in verb_docs() in Rust. A docs send for the agent returns each doc cut to its first sentence, which the clip shortens: schedule, pause and history with their arguments. A reflect of the same agent answers with no verbs and no emits.

#### The record fields a bundle reads

An agent’s **record** holds `id`, `handler_module`, `parent_id` and any other fields written to it ([Records](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/records/)). A bundle reads the fields it defines. In Python the agent object has `record` and `get(id)`. In Rust the fields are `agent.meta`, behind a lock. The scheduler reads `paused` from the record each time it decides whether to fire, and it writes the same field with `update`.

A field that only your bundle understands needs a check that only your bundle can make. That is `validate_meta(meta, record)`. `meta` is the patch, and `record` is the agent’s current fields, empty at create. Return a string to refuse the write, or nothing to accept it. The kernel calls it in both `create_agent` and `update_agent`, so a value refused on update is refused on create too. The refusal has the reason `invalid_meta`.

Judge the state the write will produce, not the patch alone. The `static_loader` reads one field, `manifest`, and checks it against the merged view.

static_loader/tools.py, validate_meta (shortened):

```
def validate_meta(meta, record):
    merged = {**record, **meta}
    if "manifest" not in merged:
        return None
    path = merged.get("manifest")
    if not isinstance(path, str) or not path:
        return "static_loader: manifest must be a non-empty path string"
```

The Rust bundle has the same method on the trait and the same text. The hook is handed no kernel, so it checks shape only. Whether the manifest file exists is a question for the verb that reads it, at boot.

A bundle can also publish what its record takes before any agent exists. Python reads a module attribute `RECORD_SCHEMA`, and Rust calls `record_schema()`. The kernel adds it to the bundle’s entry in `reflect bundles=all`. A bundle that publishes a schema enforces the same one in `validate_meta`.

*Animation: validate_meta judges the record* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle/record.mp4). The record holds manifest fantastic.yaml. An update_agent patch sets manifest to an empty string. validate_meta gets the patch and the record and refuses it with invalid_meta, manifest must be a non-empty path string, before the record changes. A patch that sets manifest to team.yaml passes, and the record changes. Create is judged the same way.

#### Hooks: what to free when the agent goes

A bundle that keeps state in the process, such as a cache or a running loop, frees it in a hook. Python looks for module functions `on_delete(agent)` and `on_shutdown(agent)`. Rust’s trait has `on_delete`, `on_shutdown` and `on_cancel`, all defaulting to nothing.

The shutdown hook is the only one the shutdown walk calls. There is no fallback to `on_delete`, so a bundle that frees resources at shutdown says so. The scheduler does it in one line, `on_shutdown = on_delete`, and Rust’s `on_shutdown` calls its own `on_delete`.

The scheduler starts its loop with `spawn_task`, so the loop is in `ps` and can be cancelled. See [Tasks](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/). A bare background task would be missing from both.

#### Passing the contract and the parity checks

The `contract/` folder states wire behaviour as data ([The contract](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/contract/)). Its `unknown-verb` case sends a verb that does not exist to a probe agent, a test fixture and not a shipped bundle, and expects `reason: unhandled`. Nothing in the contract runs against a new bundle. It pins the wire behaviour, and a bundle should answer an unknown verb the same way, with `unhandled` and the `verb` field, as both scheduler files do. The scheduler’s own parity case, `shutdown` to `unhandled`, is the per-bundle check.

Contract files that are about a kind of bundle exist for memory stores. `contract/memory_store/cases.json` says that every memory store bundle in every runtime that ships it replays its scenarios and must answer each step as written. If your bundle is a memory store, those scenarios are your cases.

For everything else, the checks are in the repository’s process. These are the steps for a bundle that has twins:

1. Write the Python bundle first, with its tests in the package’s `tests/` folder. Python is the reference.
2. Write the Rust bundle with the same verbs, the same docs, the same refusal texts and its own unit tests in `src/tests.rs`.
3. Add the verbs to the parity harness. `e2e/parity` sends the same inputs to a Python kernel and a Rust kernel and diffs the Rust answers against Python’s. Its `bundle_verbs` family has a list of cases for the scheduler, among them `{"type": "shutdown"}`, which is not a verb and must be refused alike.
4. Name the verbs and fields in the bundle’s own docs. If a change alters the wire protocol, it must land in every host; CONTRIBUTING.md says a change to one bundle’s internals with no wire impact needs no such parity.

The parity harness and the contract files live in the fantastic repository, which does not accept outside pull requests. A bundle you keep in your own repository runs the first two steps and your own selftest; the diff against Python applies when you also ship a twin.

*Animation: Three checks for a new bundle* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle/checks.mp4). A new bundle, tally.tools, meets three checks. A bundle should answer an unknown verb with unhandled, as the contract’s unknown-verb case pins on a probe agent and the scheduler’s parity case checks per bundle. The bundle’s own tests pass in each runtime it ships in: tests/ in Python and tests.rs in Rust. For a twin, the parity harness diffs the Rust answers against Python, the reference.

The bundle’s `selftest.md` is a walk through the CLI with the expected output of each step. The scheduler’s runs `fantastic <id> <verb> …` against a fresh `.fantastic` folder.

#### Where to go next

A bundle that is only a folder, with a program in any language and no new crate, is the other route; it is in [Kernel › Bundles](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/#folder-bundles) and [Program agents](/fantastic/foundations/agents/program-agents/). To see what a bundle’s agent may call and be called by, read [The call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/).

Sources: Rust: the Bundle trait and registry (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/fantastic-kernel/src/bundle.rs#L50); Python: the scheduler bundle (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/scheduler/src/scheduler/tools.py#L514); Python: the scheduler’s entry point (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/scheduler/pyproject.toml#L13); Rust: the scheduler bundle (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-scheduler/src/lib.rs#L210); Python: static_loader and validate_meta (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/loader/static_loader/src/static_loader/tools.py#L88); Rust: static_loader validate_meta (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-static-loader/src/lib.rs#L314); Python: the docs verb (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/kernel/_docs.py#L1); a bundle written outside the kernel tree (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/tree/main/src/tui/bundles/fantastic-web-mcp); the parity harness: scheduler cases (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/e2e/parity/families/bundle_verbs.py#L187); the contract: unknown-verb case (probe agent) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/contract/conformance/cases.json#L44)

### Foundations › Build your own › A program agent

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/program-agent/

A **program agent** is a folder with a program in it. This page is a walkthrough: make one from the starter, add a verb, see what a save does, and keep a copy that does not change.

What the running program sees and how it ends is on [Program agents](/fantastic/foundations/agents/program-agents/), and how a folder becomes a bundle is on [Bundles](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/#folder-bundles). This page does not repeat either.

#### Start from the starter

The CLI ships one starter, `python_agent`. On the canvas, double-click and pick **python agent**. The host copies the starter into a new folder `.fantastic/bundles/py_<hex>/` and places one instance of it, `py_<hex>_1`, with its view on the canvas. It refuses to reuse a folder name that already exists.

The folder holds four files:

- `bundle.yaml` names the base (`py_agent`), the `command` that starts the program, the `verbs` it serves with a one-line doc each, and the `record` defaults.
- `agent.py` is the program. Its verbs are the functions it passes to `fa.serve`.
- `panel.html` is the view the instance shows on the canvas.
- `fantastic_agent.py` is the reference helper, copied next to the program ([The program’s side](/fantastic/foundations/agents/program-agents/#helper)).

agent.py of the starter (comments left out):

```
import fantastic_agent as fa

count = 0

def hello(p):
    return {"greeting": f"hello, {p.get('name') or 'world'}"}

def bump(p):
    global count
    count += 1
    fa.emit({"type": "count", "count": count})
    return {"count": count}

fa.serve({"hello": hello, "count": bump})
```

The verb `hello` answers a greeting. The verb `count` adds one to a counter, emits an event with the new value, and returns it. The panel redraws on that event. `bundle.yaml` lists the same two verbs, and its `record` holds `inherit_env: [PATH]`, which is what lets the bare command `python3` be found.

*Animation: The starter becomes a bundle* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/program-agent/scaffold.mp4). A double-click on “python agent” copies four files into a new folder, bundles/py_ab12 (illustrative id): bundle.yaml, agent.py, panel.html and fantastic_agent.py. The kernel loads the bundle, and one instance, py_ab12_1, appears and runs.

#### Add a verb in two places

A verb exists in `agent.py` and in `bundle.yaml`, and the two lists must be equal. Write the function, add it to the dictionary passed to `fa.serve`, and add a line under `verbs` in `bundle.yaml`.

adding shout (illustrative verb):

```
agent.py      fa.serve({"hello": hello, "count": bump, "shout": shout})
bundle.yaml   verbs:
                hello: "args: name:str?. Returns {greeting}."
                count: "args: none. …"
                shout: "args: text:str (req). Returns {text}."
```

The program says `hello` with its sorted verb names when it starts. If they differ from `bundle.yaml`, the instance stops with “the program serves […] but bundle.yaml declares […] — they must match”, and `reflect` shows that text as `program_error`. A call to a verb that `bundle.yaml` does not list is refused as `unhandled` with the hint `its verbs: …`.

Three names are not yours: `reflect`, `boot` and `shutdown` are answered by the kernel, and declaring one in `verbs` is refused.

*Animation: A verb lives in two places* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/program-agent/verb.mp4). agent.py serves hello and count, and bundle.yaml declares the same two. Adding shout to the program alone makes its hello differ from the declaration, and the instance stops with “they must match”. Adding shout to bundle.yaml too makes the lists equal, and the instance runs.

#### Save, and every instance restarts

In the terminal host, a watcher keeps an eye on `.fantastic/bundles/`. It runs on the operating system’s file events, so nothing runs while nothing changes. Saves that arrive within 150 ms of each other count as one change. Python’s `__pycache__` files are ignored.

A change to any file of the bundle except its view makes the watcher send the kernel `reload_bundle {name}`. The kernel re-reads `bundle.yaml`, then sends `shutdown` with the reason `reloaded` and `boot` to every live instance of that bundle. The restart is abrupt: a call still in flight settles as `transport_closed`, and its message says the program was reloaded. The next call meets the new code in a new process.

A change to the view file (`panel.html`) restarts nothing. The host writes each instance’s `view` again, and the cells redraw. A change to `bundle.yaml` also reaches the `calls` list of every instance’s view, so a panel that calls a new verb is not refused.

The watcher belongs to the terminal host. `reload_bundle` itself is a kernel verb in both runtimes, answered by the root: without the watcher, send it yourself after you edit.

*Animation: A save restarts every instance* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/program-agent/save.mp4). A call is in flight on py_ab12_1 when agent.py is saved. The watcher sends reload_bundle, and the call settles as transport_closed, “reloaded”. Both instances, py_ab12_1 and py_ab12_2, restart on the new code. A save of panel.html restarts nothing and only redraws the cells.

#### Copy the folder for a release

A save changes every instance of the bundle, because the code lives in the bundle and an instance is only a record that names it. To change one agent without touching the others, fork first.

Copy the folder to a new name, for example `.fantastic/bundles/web_search`. The new name is a new handler. Its instances are not touched by edits to the original, and the original’s are not touched by edits to the copy. Every bundle in the folder appears as a tile in the double-click popup, and each pick places one more instance, `<name>_<n>`. An agent can do the same with `spawn {instance_of: <name>}`.

To update the release from the working folder later, copy the working files over the release folder. Every instance of the release then restarts with the new code.

#### What the folder is allowed to do

A program agent’s code runs with your operating-system rights. What it does itself, such as reading files, starting processes or opening the network, passes no kernel gate. Only the verbs that reach it, and the sends it makes through its agent, are gated ([Program agents](/fantastic/foundations/agents/program-agents/#out), [Security](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/security/)). A bundle is a folder of open files, so read one before you run it.

Sources: the starter: agent.py (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/agent.py#L7); the starter: bundle.yaml (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/bundle.yaml#L1); the starter: panel.html (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/panel.html#L1); the dev watcher: reload on save (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/bundle_watch.rs#L1); the starter copied into a new folder (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/bundle_watch.rs#L238); reload_bundle in Rust (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-core/src/lib.rs#L729); reload_bundle in Python (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/python/bundled_agents/loader/kernel_state/src/kernel_state/tools.py#L1109); bundles.md: make, change, keep (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/docs/bundles.md#L14)

### Foundations › Build your own › A view

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/view/

An agent shows itself through its record. Give the record a `view` that names an HTML file, and the canvas draws that file as a panel: buttons that call the agent’s verbs and a script that redraws when the agent emits an event.

This page builds one from the starter that ships with the CLI. How the app **chooses** a view is [Views of agents](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/views/). The sandbox it runs in is [HTML and GL agents](/fantastic/foundations/canvas/html-gl/). The program behind the verbs is [Program agents](/fantastic/foundations/agents/program-agents/).

#### Three files: record, verbs, panel

The starter is a **folder bundle** ([Bundles](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/bundles/#folder-bundles)). `spawn {bundle: python_agent}` copies its files into a new folder, `.fantastic/bundles/py_<hex>/`, loads it, makes one instance named `<folder>_1`, and writes the instance’s view from the bundle. Each file has one job.

| file | job |
|---|---|
| `bundle.yaml` | the verbs, and `record.view`: the view every instance gets |
| `agent.py` | the verbs. `count` adds one and calls `fa.emit({"type": "count", "count": n})` |
| `panel.html` | the view: buttons that send verbs and a `watch` that redraws |

the view record (bundle.yaml):

```
view: {kind: html, bytes_file: panel.html, calls: [hello, count, watch]}
```

`kind: html` selects the HTML view renderer (`agent_view`). `bytes_file` names the body, relative to the bundle folder. `calls` lists the verbs the body may send to its agent. The two verbs in `bundle.yaml` must equal the ones `agent.py` serves, or the kernel refuses the agent (see [Program agents](/fantastic/foundations/agents/program-agents/#start)).

A view can also carry its HTML inline as `bytes` in the record instead of `bytes_file`. With neither, the cell says the agent declares no view body.

To show the agent, call `place {backend_id: "<id>", x, y}` on the canvas’s view, with no `kind`. It makes a cell that is a view of that host agent, 480 by 320 unless the call gives a size. An unknown agent is refused as `not_found`, and a missing `x` or `y` as `bad_arg`.

#### The panel: send, watch, and {{agent}}

The panel is a fragment of HTML. The canvas wraps it in a document and puts a small script, the **connector**, in its head, so a global `fantastic` exists before the body runs. The frame is a sandboxed iframe: scripts run, but the only way out is a message to the page.

| call | does |
|---|---|
| `fantastic.send(target, payload)` | sends a message and returns a promise of the reply |
| `fantastic.watch(src, cb)` | calls `cb` with each event the agent emits; returns a function that stops watching |
| `fantastic.emit(target, payload)` | emits an event on another agent |
| `fantastic.onMessage(cb)` | receives messages sent to the cell itself |

The agent’s own id is not known when you write the file, so write `{{agent}}`. When the canvas reads the file it replaces every `{{agent}}` with the instance’s id. One `panel.html` therefore serves every instance of the bundle.

panel.html (the starter, shortened):

```
const AGENT = "{{agent}}";
document.getElementById("c").onclick =
  () => fantastic.send(AGENT, {type: "count"});
fantastic.watch(AGENT, (ev) => {
  if (ev && ev.type === "count") out.textContent = "count = " + ev.count;
});
```

The button only sends. The new number arrives as an event, because the `count` verb emits it, and the `watch` callback draws it. Any other client of the agent sees the same event. The starter never polls.

Setting `innerHTML` runs no `<script>`. Keep the script in `panel.html`, and send data, or HTML without scripts, in the events.

*Animation: A view: click, verb, event, redraw* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/view/starter.mp4). py_ab12_1 has view {kind: html, bytes_file: panel.html, calls: [hello, count, watch]}. The panel sends count to py_ab12_1 through its cell. The agent adds one and emits {type: count, count: 1}, and the panel’s watch redraws “count = 1”.

#### What the panel may call

The panel does not act as you. Its sends go out as its **cell**, which is an agent, so the [call gate](/fantastic/foundations/protocol/call-gate/) judges them like any other send. The cell’s `can_call` is derived from the view as `{<agent id>: [hello, count, watch]}`: `calls`, plus `watch`, which a view always gets.

A verb that is not in `calls` is refused at the cell, inside the panel, where nobody reads a log. If your button needs a new verb, add it to the bundle’s `verbs`, to `agent.py` and to `calls`.

The other end of the edge is the agent’s `callable_by`. The terminal UI shell grants `user`, which every canvas tab calls through, on each agent it sees, and `spawn` waits for that grant before it returns. For an agent you create by hand, the canvas’s own documentation says to give it `callable_by: {user: [the verbs the panel calls, watch]}`, because a new agent admits no one.

A chat can show the same panel inside a conversation. The AI’s `embed {id}` verb draws a card for any host agent with a `view` record, and it checks the same grants. It answers `not_found`, `no_view` or `grants_missing` with the fix in `hint`. One agent can be a chat card and a canvas cell at once.

#### Edit it while it runs

The CLI watches every bundle folder. It listens to file events rather than polling, and it treats one save, a burst of events within 150 ms, as one change. What happens depends on the file.

- **`panel.html`** (the view file): the CLI writes each instance’s `view` again, and the cells redraw. Nothing restarts.
- **`agent.py` or `bundle.yaml`**: the kernel runs `reload_bundle`. Every instance stops abruptly and starts again, and calls in flight answer `reloaded`.

The record the CLI writes takes `kind`, `calls` and `bytes_file` from `bundle.yaml` over the instance’s own. A new verb in `calls` therefore reaches every instance’s grant. It also removes any inline `bytes` and adds `bytes_rev`, a hash of the file, so the change is visible to the cells. If you save the code and the panel together, the code reloads first and then the panel redraws.

*Animation: Edit a bundle while it runs* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/view/edit.mp4). Two instances, py_ab12_1 and py_ab12_2, share one bundle. Saving panel.html redraws both cells with no restart. Saving agent.py runs reload_bundle, and both instances restart.

A bundle’s edit changes every instance. To change one agent alone, copy the folder to a new name first.

#### In the terminal UI

The terminal UI does not run `panel.html`. It has its own panel per kind of agent, chosen by the agent’s `handler_module`, and no code in its panels reads a `view` record.

A bundle you wrote has an unknown module, so the TUI shows the **generic panel**: the agent’s id, whether it is open or sealed, its sentence, the last call, its egress (`can_call`) and ingress (`callable_by`), its verbs with their argument lines, and its rows. You can call any verb it lists, and the answer, a refusal included, is shown verbatim. That is enough to try `hello` and `count` from the terminal.

*Animation: The TUI shows the generic panel* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/view/tui.mp4). py_ab12_1 is selected in the TUI tree. Its handler_module is unknown to the shell, so it gets the generic panel: sentence, verbs hello and count, and a call. count answers {count: 1}.

In the public code, `make` in `panel/mod.rs` is a fixed `match` over the panel kinds. This page therefore claims no way to add a custom TUI panel: a new handler gets the generic panel. The views you write are for the canvas.

Sources: starter bundle.yaml: the view record (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/bundle.yaml#L9); starter agent.py: a verb that emits (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/agent.py#L36); starter panel.html: send and watch (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/starters/python_agent/panel.html#L6); connector.ts: the fantastic object (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/html_agent/connector.ts#L40); agent_view.ts: reading the view file (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/agent_view/agent_view.ts#L57); host_views.ts: the cell’s grant (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/web/canvas/src/bundles/canvas/host_views.ts#L108); bundle_watch.rs: live edits and the starters (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/kern/bundle_watch.rs#L1); panel/mod.rs: the TUI panels (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/tui/src/panel/mod.rs#L78)

### Foundations › Build your own › Example: Team

URL: https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/team/

[fantastic_team](https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team) is a separate, public program built on fantastic. Its README describes it as unattended team work: you queue tasks, a team of AI workers takes them, and you review what comes back. It is an example of what the pieces on the other pages make when you put them together.

This page follows four parts of it: how `team.yaml` turns role cards into agents, what the `project_lead` card grants and asks, how the lead records its work in the task registry, and what the cadencer sends back up. Everything about fantastic itself is covered on the pages linked in each section; this page shows Team’s use of it. The statements about Team come from its repository at the commit named in the sources.

#### What Team is, and what it is not yet

Team depends on fantastic as a pinned git dependency, so it uses the same kernel, agents and bundles described in the other Foundations pages. A **team** is a folder with a `team.yaml`. The file names the worker templates the team may start, the connectors it may use, the queue and the credential store.

The binary adds no coding agent of its own. A `team.yaml` with no `templates` and no `first_agent` is valid and starts only the system agents: the dispatcher, the tools and the queue. Which agents exist is the file’s choice.

- The README says there are no releases yet, so you build from source with `sh scripts/build.sh`. It needs `git` and a Rust toolchain.
- It also says CI runs the unit tests on Linux, macOS and Windows, but the run was verified on Linux only.
- Team does not merge. A worker opens a draft pull request, and a person reviews and merges it.

#### Role cards and tiers in team.yaml

Team turns on fantastic’s roles registry with a `roles:` section. It takes an `id` (default `roles`), `dirs`, the folders of role cards (default `roles`), and `limits` with `total` and `per_role`. Team applies the limits with `set_limit` at every start, and clears a limit the file no longer names. [Agentic resources and tasks](/fantastic/foundations/agents/agentic-resources/) explains the registry; the cards and limits themselves work as described there.

the roles section of examples/team.yaml:

```
roles:
  id: roles
  dirs: [roles]
  limits:
    total: 3
    per_role:
      worker: 2
```

A card’s `tier` is the name of a template in the same `team.yaml`. A card therefore names no model: the file maps the tier to a model, an endpoint and a credential, and the registry holds one tier per template. The example file names three tiers, `strong`, `small` and `issue_keeper`. A test checks that no card text names a provider or a model.

Team ships six cards in its `roles/` folder. The `project_lead` card replaces fantastic’s generic card of the same name.

| card | tier | grants |
|---|---|---|
| `worker` | `small` | `worker_exec`, `worker_files`, `queue` |
| `lead` | `strong` | `$registry`, `worker_exec`, `worker_files`, `queue`, `kernel` |
| `project_lead` | `strong` | `$registry`, `github`, `board`, `queue`, `kernel_state`, `tasks` |
| `issue_keeper` | `issue_keeper` | `queue` |
| `issue_writer` | `small` | `queue` |
| `spec_reviewer` | `small` | `queue`, `worker_files` |

Team checks the cards before it starts. It refuses to start when a card does not parse, names a tier that is not a template, grants an agent that `team.yaml` does not define, or when one of the six cards is missing. `roles:` also needs a `first_agent` and `templates`.

*Animation: Cards name a tier, team.yaml defines it* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/team/cards.mp4). team.yaml defines templates, here strong and small. The project_lead card names strong and the worker card names small, so no card names a model. A third card, reviewer, names tier fast. No template has that name, so the team refuses to start.

#### The project lead plans a tree

The `project_lead` card describes a lead that “plans a team’s open issues as a tree of agents, runs it through the GitHub connector, and reports one condensed account upward”. It plans and coordinates, and does not write code. Its grants are the whole of what it can do:

| grant | verbs |
|---|---|
| `$registry` | `roles`, `role`, `spawn`, `get_count`, `fleet`, `report` |
| `github` | `issues`, `issue_view`, `issue_edit`, `issue_state`, `comment`, `label`, `project_field_set`, `pr_create`, `pr_status`, `staleness`, `push` |
| `board` | `board`, `rows` |
| `queue` | all verbs |
| `kernel_state` | `await_set`, `await_cancel` |
| `tasks` | `add`, `assign`, `reassign`, `status`, `report`, `list`, `get` |

The card tells it a flow. It reads the issues and the board, and it reads its own room: `roles`, `get_count` and the fork points of its conversation. It then proposes a tree in the chat: sub-leads per area, a worker per issue, what waits on what. After approval it grows the tree with `spawn {role, task}` on the registry. A sub-lead starts with `spawn {role, from: {agent, at}}`, which branches off a mark in the lead’s conversation ([Forking and marks](/fantastic/foundations/agents/ai-agent/forking/)), and with `limits` that hand it part of the lead’s quota ([the quota](/fantastic/foundations/agents/agentic-resources/#quotas)).

It waits for its children with `await_set` ([Tasks and waiting](/fantastic/foundations/kernel/tasks/)), never with a shell wait or short polling loops. Team writes the other end of that grant at every start: it names the agents below the root in the root’s `callable_by` with `await_set` and `await_cancel`.

#### When it asks first

The card says when to stop and ask. It asks before a plan of more than five agents, before going past its limits, and before any GitHub write (`issue_edit`, `issue_state`, `comment`, `label`, `pr_create`, `push`). A small plan within its limits and with no GitHub write may start at once. If the user says “show me the plan first”, it always waits for a “yes”.

> Approval is the user's reply in the chat, nothing else: no button, no code gate. (roles/project_lead.md)

This is a rule in the card’s text, which the model reads. Team’s tests check that the card contains these rules, but no code enforces the wait. What code does enforce is the grants: a call the card does not list is refused with “may not call”, and the card tells the lead to say so and stop. The limits are enforced too. A spawn past a limit is refused, and the card says that refusal is final.

Nothing is cleaned up until the user asks. The lead never deletes an agent or closes an issue by itself, so finished agents, their histories and their marks stay. The card has each worker make a branch, push it and open a draft pull request through the `github` connector, and the lead reads the worker’s ticks and labels instead of redoing them. The shipped `worker` card grants no connector, so a team whose workers deliver this way adds `github` to its own worker card.

*Animation: The project lead grows a tree* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/team/plan.mp4). The project lead proposes a plan of six agents in the chat (the project lead and five it will start). Over five agents, so it waits. The user replies yes. It spawns a sub-lead and workers through the registry, and records each issue in tasks with a holder: w1 holds o/r#12, and the sub-lead’s subtree holds the rest of its area.

#### Tasks it records

With `roles:`, Team adds one more agent, `tasks`: fantastic’s `task_registry`, created as a child of the lead. The id `tasks` is taken. Its rows live in the team’s one store agent, a `sqlite_store` whose file is `.fantastic/memory.db` by default. That store also keeps every AI agent’s conversation, so the history and the task rows survive a restart.

The card tells the project lead to record each issue it hands out. Right after it starts an agent for an issue, it calls `add` with the issue as the `source` and the agent as the `holder`. When it gives a whole area to a sub-lead, the holder is that sub-lead’s subtree. When it hands an issue to another agent, it calls `reassign`, and the registry keeps every step in the task’s history.

illustrative ids: the lead’s calls on tasks:

```
add {"id": "o/r#12", "source": "gh:o/r#12", "holder": "w1"}
reassign {"id": "o/r#12", "holder": {"subtree": "sub-a"}}
```

The card also has the lead store, with each task, the `versions` it was done against (`{repo, branch, commit}` per repo), the issue’s `source_version`, and the mark it was forked from (`fork_from`). Before it reuses a mark, it calls the connector’s `staleness` verb, which returns the commits and changed files since the recorded commit and whether the issue changed. The card says “Code gives the facts; you decide”, so the choice between forking and starting fresh stays with the lead. A child’s `usage` goes up with its `report`, and `list` sums it.

The registry does not sync with GitHub. The card says so: after the lead changes a task, it pushes the update to the source itself, with `issue_edit`, `comment` or `label` on the `github` connector, at the task’s `update_to`. [Who holds what](/fantastic/foundations/agents/agentic-resources/#tasks) covers the verbs and refusals such as `already_held`.

With `roles:`, the `board` verb returns a `roles` section as well: the tree below the project lead with each agent’s role and state, the count from `get_count`, and the task rows with source, holder and status. Team finds the project lead as the first agent that the registry’s `fleet` lists under the role `project_lead`. Its end-to-end test spawns that role through the registry as the operator.

#### The cadencer reports upward

The **cadencer** is an agent Team creates in every team. It is on by default; `cadencer: {enabled: false}` creates it switched off. On a timer it reads the tree and sends each lead a short digest of the level directly below it. A sub-lead’s line rolls up its whole subtree, so a project lead sees one line per sub-lead and does not see the workers below.

In a team with `roles:`, the tree is the spawned tree. The cadencer reads the registry’s `fleet` and `get_count`, the root’s `reflect` of the project lead’s branch, and the task registry’s `list`. An agent holding a running, waiting or blocked task, itself or through an ancestor’s subtree, is busy. An agent whose tasks are all done is done, and an agent with no task is idle. Before each beat the cadencer is let `send` to the leads the registry lists under `project_lead` and `lead`, so a lead spawned after the start still gets its digest.

- The beat is 60 seconds by default. A group in `team.yaml` may set its own `cadence`, `stall_after`, `quiet` and `enabled`.
- A worker is **stalled** when it holds a task and has been idle for `stall_after` seconds (300 by default). The digest line says `STALLED` with the idle time.
- In quiet mode, the default, a digest holds only what changed since the last one, plus every stall. An empty digest is not sent.
- A quiet lead that gets no digest, has an idle member and sees queued work gets one line on every third such beat: `heartbeat: N idle, M queued`. A regular digest restarts the count.

a sub-lead’s roll-up line (illustrative values):

```
sub-a: 2 agents (2 busy) · +0 new · 1 STALLED
```

A digest goes to the lead’s driver, else to the lead itself if it has an AI, else to the board. It is a `send` whose text is the lines. A failed send is counted and is never fatal. The cadencer also reports the team’s load as plain counts in its `status`: workers busy, idle and stalled, and tasks held, in review, done, blocked and queued. The code gives only these numbers; it has no mode and no progress bar.

*Animation: The cadencer sends one line per branch* (https://aisixteen.com/fantastic/foundations/build/team/digest.mp4). The cadencer reads the spawned tree: lead, sub-lead sub-a, and two workers. Worker w2 holds a task and has been idle past stall_after. The digest to the lead has one roll-up line for sub-a with 1 STALLED, and none for the workers below.

#### Where to read more

The repository is [aisixteen/fantastic_team](https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team), under AGPL-3.0-or-later like fantastic. Start with `README.md`, `examples/team.yaml` and the six cards in `roles/`. The code for the tree, the grants and the cadencer is in `crates/team/src`. The README also covers Team’s other parts, such as the dispatcher page, worker packs and remote running, which this page leaves out.

To build your own agents of the same kind, see [A program agent](/fantastic/foundations/build/program-agent/) and [A bundle](/fantastic/foundations/build/bundle/). The cards, the registry and the task registry are the pieces that Team shares with any other team you write.

Sources: fantastic_team README: configure, roles, load and progress (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team/blob/main/README.md#L129); fantastic_team: examples/team.yaml (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team/blob/main/examples/team.yaml#L1); fantastic_team: the project_lead card (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team/blob/main/roles/project_lead.md#L1); fantastic_team: card checks and the tasks agent in the plan (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team/blob/main/crates/team/src/tree.rs#L154); fantastic_team: the cadencer (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team/blob/main/crates/team/src/cadencer.rs#L1); fantastic_team: the board’s roles section (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic_team/blob/main/crates/team/src/board.rs#L868); fantastic: the roles registry (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-agentic-resources/src/lib.rs#L88); fantastic: the task registry (Rust) (https://github.com/aisixteen/fantastic/blob/main/src/lib/rust/crates/bundles/fantastic-task-registry/src/lib.rs#L92)

## Apps

Every app: no account, no subscription, no personal data collected. Downloaded from the Apple App Store.

### Ephemeris Sky

URL: https://aisixteen.com/ephemeris-sky/ · App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6782659268
Category: Sky & science · Platforms: iPhone, iPad & Mac

The sky, computed for any moment. Natal charts, transits, synastry and returns — computed on your device.

Turn any moment into a precise picture of the solar system. Ephemeris Sky computes real geocentric planetary positions, the aspects between them, and a live chart wheel for any date and time. Save your natal chart and read today’s sky against it, compare two charts with synastry that ranks every contact, score dignities and see the balance of a chart, and get the next solar or lunar return to the minute. Choose your house system — Placidus, Koch, Whole Sign and more — and follow an event timeline of ingresses, lunations and aspects.

- Your natal chart, saved in your own iCloud, with today’s transits
- Synastry — two charts, every contact ranked
- Dignities and balance, scored and ranked, with the shape of the chart
- Solar and lunar returns to the minute, plus an event timeline

Privacy: On-device, no account, works offline.

**Does Ephemeris Sky work offline?** Yes. Every calculation runs on your device, so it works with no internet connection. Anything you save syncs through your own iCloud whenever a connection is available.

**Is there an account or subscription?** No. There's no sign-up, no login, and no subscription — just download Ephemeris Sky from the App Store and open it.

**What data does Ephemeris Sky collect?** None. There are no accounts, no analytics and no tracking, and we receive nothing. Anything you save is stored in your own private iCloud container, not on our servers.

**Which devices are supported?** Ephemeris Sky is available for iPhone, iPad & Mac.

### Marine Nav

URL: https://aisixteen.com/marine-nav/ · App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6795571481
Category: Sky & science · Platforms: iPhone, iPad & Mac

Tides, currents and celestial navigation. Offline tide and tidal-current predictions, sight reduction, and magnetic declination.

An offline navigation toolkit for sailors and navigators. Predict tide heights and tidal currents — including slack water — work a celestial sight from sextant altitude to a fix, read magnetic declination from the World Magnetic Model, and solve great-circle distance and bearing. Everything is computed on your device from published data, so it keeps working with no signal at sea.

- Tide heights and tidal currents, with slack water
- Celestial sight reduction — sextant altitude to a fix
- Magnetic declination from the World Magnetic Model
- Great-circle distance & bearing · 100% offline

Privacy: On-device, no account, works offline.

**Does Marine Nav work offline?** Yes. Marine Nav runs entirely on your device, so it works with no internet connection.

**Is there an account or subscription?** No. There's no sign-up, no login, and no subscription — just download Marine Nav from the App Store and open it.

**What data does Marine Nav collect?** None. It collects, stores, and transmits zero personal data — nothing ever leaves your device.

**Which devices are supported?** Marine Nav is available for iPhone, iPad & Mac.

### Par

Category: Creative tools · Platforms: iPhone, iPad & Mac

The financial calculator that cites its sources. Ten tools — time value of money, bonds, amortization, cash flow and more.

An offline financial calculator for people who must have one: loan officers, mortgage and commercial real-estate underwriters, treasury and fixed-income desks, and candidates studying where only a financial calculator is permitted. Ten tools cover time value of money, amortization, bonds, cash flow, day count, depreciation, percent, rate conversion, real estate, and statistics — and every displayed number traces to a cited authority.

- Ten tools: TVM, amortization, bonds, cash flow, depreciation & more
- Every result cites its authority — US Treasury, CFPB Reg Z & DD, IRS, NIST
- A running tape of your calculations you can review and save
- One-time purchase · no ads, no subscription, no account, no network

Layout, lumber and takeoff, on site. Tape math, on-center layout, board feet, roof pitch and takeoff — all offline.

A job-site calculator for carpenters, framers and remodelers. Run feet-inch-fraction tape math, lay out equal spacing and on-center marks, size lumber in board feet with nominal-versus-dressed dimensions, work roof pitch and rafters, square up and solve miters and bevels, take off concrete in cubic yards, and check wire gauge. Everything runs on your device — including on your wrist, right at the wall.

### AirCore

URL: https://aisixteen.com/aircore/ · App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6799999307
Category: Creative tools · Platforms: iPhone, iPad, Mac & Apple Watch

The offline air-side HVAC calculator. Psychrometrics, duct, fan and pipe in one app — corrected for your site elevation, not sea level.

The air-side calculator for HVAC technicians, designers and contractors. Enter any two of dry bulb, wet bulb, dew point, relative humidity, humidity ratio, enthalpy or specific volume and AirCore solves the rest, putting the point on a real psychrometric chart — type a value and the point moves, drag the point and the values follow. Site elevation sits in the toolbar of every screen and every number is corrected to it, so you are not quietly working at sea level. Imperial and metric switch freely without re-rounding, and the physics lives in independently tested modules checked against published reference data.

- Any two knowns solve the whole air state, plotted on a real chart
- Corrected for your site elevation — see what the altitude costs
- Air-side heat in any direction, and air mixing weighted by mass
- Duct from friction, fan laws, and pipe by Darcy or Hazen–Williams

Privacy: On-device, no account, works offline.

**Does AirCore work offline?** Yes. AirCore runs entirely on your device, so it works with no internet connection.

**Is there an account or subscription?** No. There's no sign-up, no login, and no subscription — just download AirCore from the App Store and open it.

**What data does AirCore collect?** None. It collects, stores, and transmits zero personal data — nothing ever leaves your device.

**Which devices are supported?** AirCore is available for iPhone, iPad, Mac & Apple Watch.
